Embeddings Retention & Tiered Storage PRD Overview: This PRD defines a system for configurable retention and tiered storage for customer embeddings stored in Redwood Inference. The goal is to reduce per-customer storage cost, control long-term operational expense, and provide clear controls for compliance (data deletion/retention) while preserving retrieval latency and quality for production retrieval workloads. Background and problem statement: - Customers increasingly store large collections of vectors (embeddings) for semantic search, personalization, agent memory, and analytics. - Hot storage costs are rising as vector stores grow; many vectors are infrequently accessed but must often be retained for regulatory or business reasons. - Current single-tier storage forces a cost/latency tradeoff: keep everything hot (low latency, high cost) or move to cold (low cost, high latency and reindexing overhead). - Operators need predictable unit economics per embedding, and product teams need customer-facing controls to tune retention vs cost. Objectives (must): 1. Provide a tiered storage model with at least three tiers: HOT (low-latency SSD), WARM (object store + approximate index), and COLD (archival object store). 2. Expose customer-configurable retention policies (time-based TTL, usage-based decay, manual labels) with safe defaults and per-tenant overrides. 3. Maintain retrieval SLOs for HOT and WARM tiers: HOT 95th pct <= 50ms for top-k queries; WARM 95th pct <= 350ms for cached ANN fallthrough. 4. Implement transparent billing adjustments and meter usage by storage tier and API access pattern. 5. Provide admin tooling for forced deletion, export, and evidence of deletion for compliance. ADR - Tiered Fidelity Runtime Contract Summary: This ADR defines the 'Tiered Fidelity' runtime contract: a minimal, extensible API and runtime surface that lets clients request coarse-grained fidelity levels for inference (premium, standard, budget). The contract ties API semantics to implementation expectations across runtime, scheduling, autoscaling, observability, and cost accounting so teams can reliably reason about latency, accuracy, and unit cost tradeoffs. Context and problem: - Multiple product teams have independently exposed heuristics for lowering inference cost (aggressive quantization, batched early-exits, relaxed decoding) with no consistent client contract. - Operators lack per-fidelity telemetry, which makes SLO attribution, capacity planning, and regressions noisy and slow to troubleshoot. - Private and Dedicated deployments need a predictable mapping between client intent (latency vs fidelity) and runtime behaviour that can be overridden by admin policies. Decision (what we adopt): We introduce a small, stable contract with these elements: 1) API field: fidelity_level (optional string enum). Valid values: "premium", "standard", "budget". Omitted -> "standard". 2) Behavioral intent per value (non-prescriptive implementation surface): - premium: prioritize fidelity and determinism. Expect strict sampling (temperature control), conservative quantization, smaller batch sizes, and increased CPU/GPU reservation. Target SLO (short-context, 256 tokens): p95 <= 700ms; cost multiplier <= 1.6x. - standard: balanced baseline behavior. Target SLO: p95 <= 400ms; cost multiplier = 1.0x. - budget: prioritize cost and throughput; allow larger batches, lower-precision kernels and opportunistic early-exit. Target SLO: p95 <= 220ms; cost multiplier <= 0.55x. 3) Implementation mapping: runtime will map the tuple (model_id, fidelity_level, workload_signature) -> fidelity_profile_id. Profiles

ADR: Fidelity tiering and degraded-pathing topology Summary: This ADR defines a topology and runtime contract for fidelity tiering and degraded-pathing across Redwood's inference surface. The goal is to provide deterministic, observable, and auditable trade-offs between latency/cost and model output fidelity so product teams can accept documented degradations under capacity, cost-control, or region-failover scenarios. Context and motivation: - Production workloads vary: some calls are latency-critical (autocomplete, chat-turns), others are cost-dominant (bulk-embeddings, nightly reranks). - We must be able to steer requests toward lower-cost or lower-fidelity variants without introducing silent quality regressions. - Existing fallback patterns handle single-version fallbacks; we need a multi-tier topology with clear telemetry, SLA composition, and rollout controls. Decision: topology and contracts We adopt a 3-tier fidelity topology with an explicit controller and policy layer: 1) Fidelity tiers (logical): - fidelity:high — full-precision model, full decoding, KV cache warm, no quantization; primary for high-quality routes. SLO: P50 latency <= 60ms, P95 <= 150ms; Availability: 99.9% - fidelity:balanced — mixed precision / 8-bit quant, CPU fallback allowed for cold sequences, limited response length; SLO: P50 <= 90ms, P95 <= 250ms - fidelity:degraded — aggressive quantization + prompt-preserving compression, early-exit heuristics, truncated decoding; SLO: P95 <= 500ms; Quality budget: max 12% drop on normalized eval metric (model-specific). 2) Runtime components and responsibilities: - fidelity-controller (service): evaluates routing policy, enforces per-tenant fidelity caps, and emits routing decisions. Owner: eng-serving-runtime. - model-variants (runtime group): deployments of the same model artifact with different execution profiles (precision, kernel set, KV behavior). Owner: eng-platform. -

Affinity Contracts and Fidelity Boundaries: product guide and rollout plan Executive summary: This document introduces the "Affinity Contract" concept and the related notion of Fidelity Boundaries. Affinity Contracts are a customer-visible contract describing how traffic will be routed, cached, and served across edge/hosted/dedicated surfaces to meet latency and cost objectives. Fidelity Boundaries define the observable guarantees for output quality under constrained capacity or cheaper execution modes (e.g., quantized variants, distilled models, or cached prefix completion). Goals: - Provide product definitions that let customers select predictable trade-offs (latency vs cost vs fidelity). - Surface a simple contract model that the API, Console, and Billing can reference. - Define requirements, telemetry, and rollout plan so engineering and GTM can deliver an initial MVP for Dedicated and Hosted in Q1 2026. Problem statement: Many customers need predictable behavior when inference capacity is constrained (bursting, regional outages, or deliberate cost-saving fallbacks). Past incidents and feedback highlight three recurring issues: 1) opaque fallbacks which change output quality without notifying the application; 2) difficulty mapping pricing tiers to observed fidelity; 3) lack of a migration path between hosted and Dedicated with consistent expectations. Definitions (product terms): - Affinity Contract: a declarative attachment that ties a tenant (or route) to a routing policy, cache affinity (local vs global), and an ordered fallback set of model variants. PRD: Session-Anchored Embeddings Cache and Metering Summary ------- This PRD defines a productized feature: a session-anchored embeddings cache with integrated metering and TTL tiers. The feature provides low-latency, cost-efficient vector retrieval for conversational and transactional workloads by keeping short-lived, session-scoped vectors hot while retaining an economical long-term tier for reuse and billing reconciliation. The goal is to reduce per-request embedding compute, improve tail latency for conversational flows, and introduce clear metering semantics for session-resident vectors. Background and motivation ------------------------- - Many customers run conversational agents that repeatedly re-query or augment a short-lived context (e.g., user session, chat thread). Generating embeddings repeatedly for the same context increases token and compute costs and increases latency. - Existing incremental embeddings tiering work focuses on storage durability and long-term retention; there is a gap for short-lived, session-anchored caches that are both performance-optimized and correctly metered. - Business asks: 1) reduce host inference spend for ephemeral high-QPS sessions, 2) offer predictable billing for cached embeddings (distinct from permanent storage), 3) instrument quality and eviction metrics for SRE/product monitoring. Goals ----- - Provide an in-platform session-anchored cache with three TTL tiers (session-hot: 0-30 minutes, session-warm: 30m-24h, persistent: >24h) configurable per-tenant. - Expose a clear metering model: cached-hit credits for session-hot/warm usage and standard embedding credits for persistent or cache-miss generation. - Keep additional tail latency for embed requests under 20ms P95 for session-hot cache on Dedicated and Hosted tiers. - Provide SDK primitives and server-side hooks so customers can opt into session anchoring with a single

models. Scope and user stories Primary persona: platform engineers and data platform leads at customers who run large-scale semantic search and retrieval over historical data. User stories: 1) As a customer platform engineer, I want embeddings older than 90 days to be automatically moved to a cold tier so my monthly bill decreases without manual intervention. 2) As an SRE, I want to observe migration throughput, error rates, and per-tenant cold item counts to troubleshoot performance regressions. 3) As a product analyst, I want a conservative cost-savings estimate per tenant exposed in Console before enabling tiering. Requirements Functional requirements: - FR-1: Tier definitions. System must support at least three configurable tiers: hot (SSD NVMe), warm (standard SSD), cold (object storage with optional retrieval latency up to 2s). - FR-2: Policy engine. Allow per-tenant TTL-based and access-frequency policies (e.g., move to cold after 90 days or after 30 days without a read). - FR-3: Transparent reads. Reads for cold items must be transparently proxied: if a record is in cold, the service must fetch and return the embedding without requiring client-side changes. - FR-4: Incremental migration. Support incremental background migration with rate limiting and backpressure to avoid saturating network or CPU on storage nodes. - FR-5: Compaction and dedup. Provide a periodic compaction job to detect identical embeddings and collapse duplicates to save space in cold tier (subject to privacy labels). - FR-6: Auditability. Service Fidelity, Cost Tradeoffs, and SLO Matrix Framework Overview This document defines a pragmatic framework for reasoning about service fidelity, per-request cost, and SLO placement across Redwood Inference's serving surface. It codifies a matrix for mapping request classes to SLO/budget pairs, prescribes API-level hints to enable runtime cost/fidelity negotiation, and provides an operational rollout and measurement playbook. The goal is to make tradeoffs repeatable, observable, and reversible. Why this exists (Motivation) - Rising model heterogeneity (full-precision, quantized, distilled variants) and multi-modal endpoints demand explicit guidance on when to sacrifice fidelity to save cost. - Customers require predictable unit economics; teams need standard controls for graceful quality degradation under constrained capacity. - Existing standards cover SLOs and fallback but do not specify a cross-cutting mapping from request intent -> fidelity budget -> runtime config. Scope - Applies to all Redwood runtime surfaces: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments. - Targets text generation, chat sessions, and embedding requests. Does not change model artifacts or evaluation standards; it augments serving and API semantics. Definitions - Fidelity tier: qualitative label representing expected output quality (e.g., "high-precision", "balanced", "fast-safe"). - Cost budget: expected token or GPU cost per request (USD/normalized-unit) or a relative multiplier. - Request class: classification of a call by business intent (e.g., transactional, exploratory, background-batch). - Negotiation hint: API-level field that signals client preference along latency/cost/fidelity axes. Workload-aware batching defaults (Fast / Standard / Cost-efficient) — design ## Overview This document defines Redwood Runtime’s “workload-aware batching defaults”: three customer-facing latency SLO tiers (Fast / Standard / Cost-efficient) implemented as tiered batching profiles selected automatically by the runtime based on workload signals and policy configuration. The primary goal is to reduce cost per 1K tokens via safer batching defaults while preserving predictable tail latency (especially for streaming) and avoiding starvation under mixed workloads. This is the primary design doc for: - Tier definitions and the contract we uphold for each tier (in runtime terms). - Scheduler knob mapping (continuous batching heuristics, queueing, prefill/decode balancing, admission control). - Workload signals (length buckets, streaming flag, concurrency, overload signals) and selection logic. - Override hierarchy (customer override > route/model policy > tier default) and explainability (reason codes). - Rollout and rollback plan for Hosted and Dedicated. ## Background and decision summary We will ship three tiered defaults rather than per-tenant real-time autotuning (see ADR-023). The tiers give customers a stable mental model and enable us to publish and validate recommended profiles per model family + hardware class. Key principles: 1) Tail latency is a first-class constraint (Fast tier must protect p99 and streaming “time-to-first-token”). 2) Defaults must be explainable (operators can see the effective tier/profile and why it was selected). 3) Behavior under overload must be safe and predictable (backpressure, load shedding, and bounded queues). 4) Profiles must work under mixed workloads (avoid starving long prompts, avoid “short prompts dominate forever”).

standard: balanced baseline behavior. Target SLO: p95 <= 400ms; cost multiplier = 1.0x. - budget: prioritize cost and throughput; allow larger batches, lower-precision kernels and opportunistic early-exit. Target SLO: p95 <= 220ms; cost multiplier <= 0.55x. 3) Implementation mapping: runtime will map the tuple (model_id, fidelity_level, workload_signature) -> fidelity_profile_id. Profiles are implementation artifacts that list kernel choices, quantization, batch_bounds, KV eviction hints, and decode-strategy. 4) Fallback semantics: if exact profile cannot be served, runtime should attempt, by default: same-model alternate profile -> same-family compatible model -> catalog failover model -> return 503. All fallback steps must be recorded on the response and as trace tags. 5) Policy overrides: tenant-level admin policies may pin fidelity for a tenant or promote/demote a requested level. Overridden fidelity must be returned in response metadata. 6) Observability contract: every inference request must emit structured telemetry including: request_id, fidelity_level (requested), fidelity_profile_id (applied), model_id, variant_id, decode_strategy, tokens_in, tokens_out, server_latency_ms, fallback_chain. These are strings/numeric fields and must be present as trace tags and as metric labels where cardinality permits. 7) Error attribution: SLO violations and fallback counts are attributible to the applied fidelity_profile_id and the tenant. Rationale: - A small enum surface limits client complexity while exposing a meaningful knob for cost/latency tradeoffs. - The fidelity_profile abstraction decouples client-facing stability from implementation evolution (new kernels, quant levels) allowing runtime teams to iterate without client churn. - Including policy overrides and explicit fallback recording reduces surprises for customers and makes billing and postmortems tractable. Developer Docs: Authoring Gateway and Offline Release Playbook Overview:

This playbook defines the Authoring Gateway pattern for Redwood developer docs: a lightweight pipeline and set of conventions that let contributors edit SDK guides, API examples, and docs-site snippets offline, validate them locally, and release changes through a staged rollout with automated checks and canonical fixes for top support issues. The goal is to reduce merge/revert cycles, shrink hotfix blast radius, and standardize how doc fixes for common support problems are produced and released.

Scope:
- Applies to: SDK guides, API examples, quickstarts, snippet libraries, and docs-site content under eng-developer-experience.
- Excludes: private customer-runbooks in customer repos, legal/policy documents (use policies-and-process).

Why this exists:
- Many fixes originate in support tickets and require a fast, low-risk path to publish corrected snippets and guidance.
- Offline authoring reduces friction for contributors in restricted networks or with flaky CI.
- A repeatable release orchestration (canary -> staging -> global) reduces regressions and enables targeted rollbacks.

Roles & Ownership:
- Documentation author (author-team): creates/edits content, runs local checks, opens PR.
- Docs oncall (rotation): triages release failures and coordinates emergency hotfixes.
- DX Release Engineer (owner_team: engineering): approves staged rollouts, manages release pipeline.
- Reviewers: subject-matter experts for SDK or API area (listed on PR).

title: "Streaming fallback: client resilience patterns"
affected_versions: "sdk-1.x, sdk-2.0"
labels: ["sdk","resilience","example"]
```

2) Preflight checks (local):
 - Run local validator: tools/docs-validate --spell --links

Before a docs-site change reaches production, it must go through specific review approvals, automated CI verification, and staged publishing gates:

### 1. PR Review and Approvals
* **Reviewers:** 
  * Small changes can be merged by Docs Triage with one reviewer, while larger changes require two reviewers, including a technical writer [5].
  * Changes involving APIs or behavior require at least one Developer Experience (DX) engineer and one product-owner reviewer [2].
  * Code-containing pages or snippets must be reviewed by at least one SDK team engineer/owner, who verifies snippet correctness across multiple languages when applicable [3, 7].
* **PR Requirements:** Authors submit a PR (often targeting `staging-docs` or `main`) using standard templates, detailing problem statements, reproducer steps, tests run, rollback notes, and telemetry ticket markers [1, 7].

### 2. Automated CI Checks
PRs must pass automated CI gates prior to merge, which include:
* Markdown and style linting (`docs-lint`, `yarn lint:md`, ESLint/remark-lint) [1, 2, 5, 7].
* Snippet runner/smoke tests ensuring all code samples compile and execute [1, 2, 5, 7].
* Link checking and accessibility checks [1, 2, 7].
* Telemetry annotation verification to ensure associated support tickets are referenced [1].

### 3. Canary and Staging Gating
Once PRs are merged, changes are staged through progressive release gates rather than deployed directly to production:
* **Canary Phase:** 
  * Content is deployed to a canary URL (e.g., `dev.docs.redwood.ai/canary`) or exposed to a small subset (e.g., 5%) of live traffic [1, 3, 5].
  * It undergoes a canary window (e.g., 1 hour), where observability metrics, page load metrics, and snippet execution rates (SLO $\ge$ 99%) are monitored [1].
* **Staging Phase:** 
  * If canary checks pass, content is promoted to an internal staging environment (e.g., `dev.docs.redwood.ai/staging` or `staging.docs.redwood.com`) [1, 2, 3].
  * It enters a staging window (typically 24 hours) for internal review by Product, Support, or the Docs Site Maintainer [1, 2].
  * Smoke tests are conducted to verify that canonical pages render, search indexing is updated, and critical SDK snippets execute [5, 8].

### 4. Production Promotion
* **Approvals & Window:** Production promotion requires sign-off from the Docs Site Maintainer / Docs Release Manager, or two reviewers (author + docs engineer) [2, 7, 8]. Standard promotion windows occur Monday–Friday, 9:00–17:00 PT [8].
* **Rollout:** Promotion is triggered via the release pipeline (e.g., `docs-publish --target=global --from=staging` or promote scripts with `--to=prod`) [1, 5, 8]. The rollout typically begins with low-traffic release before full propagation across the CDN, followed by at least 30 minutes of operational SLO monitoring [1, 8].

retrieved_chunks.content: Capacity Guardrails: Multitenant Throttle Governor and Eviction Escrow Runbook Summary ------- This runbook documents Redwood's operational playbook for a cluster-level throttle governor and the complementary eviction escrow mechanism used to protect SLOs during multitenant capacity shortfalls. It translates SLO and error budget signals into deterministic actions (rate-limits, admission-control, short lived evictions) while minimizing blast radius and preserving customer fairness. Scope ----- - Applies to multi-tenant inference clusters running the inference-serving runtime (service names: inference-gateway, kv-router, batch-allocator). - Covers detection, automated mitigation (throttle governor), short-lived eviction via "eviction escrow", manual overrides, and post-incident verification. - Does NOT replace tenant contract eviction policies for committed Dedicated customers; those follow dedicated-eviction-procedure page. Objectives ---------- - Maintain customer-facing SLOs: 99th percentile latency < 350ms for standard tier; availability >= 99.9%. - Keep error budget burn rate below 3x sustained for > 30 minutes before aggressive action. - Ensure predictable, auditable eviction decisions with reversible escrow state. Ownership and Contacts ---------------------- - Runbook owner: eng-sre (oncall: inference-cluster-pager) - Primary contacts: Elena Kim (SRE), Marcus Li (Platform), Priya Nair (Runtime) - Pager escalation: inference-pager -> platform-lead -> eng-sre-manager (see /oncall-and-incident-response/oncall-rotations) Key Signals and Telemetry ------------------------- 1) SLO and error budget signals - service.slo.latency.99p (ms) - service.slo.availability.rolling_1h (%) - service.error_budget.burn_rate.5m 2) Capacity signals - gpu.utilization.percent per pool - queue.wait_time.p95 (ms) - inflight_requests per tenant 3) Admission & throttling signals - admission.rejection.rate - token_bucket.fill_level (per priority-slice) Threshold table (example) ------------------------- | Trigger | Observed signal | Immediate action | |---------|-----------------|-----------------| | Warning | burn_rate >= 1.5x sustained 10m

Notifications ----------------------------------- - All throttle adjustments and eviction escrow events must be tagged with change-id and persisted to the capacity-audit-store (retention 90 days). - Billing: evictions during non-committed windows will trigger a credit evaluation; finance notifies customers according to the Customer Impact policy. Tenant burst absorber and eviction strategy Summary ------- This operational playbook documents a repeatable, low-risk pattern for absorbing short-duration tenant bursts in private (VPC / on-prem) deployments and executing targeted eviction when necessary. The goal is to preserve global SLOs (p90 latency <= 120ms, error rate <= 0.5%) while minimizing user-visible degradation and preserving tenant isolation guarantees. Scope ----- - Applies to Redwood Private control-plane + runtime deployments running the inference node pool with KV cache and model hot-swap support. - Focused on short-to-medium bursts (minutes to hours) and chronic elevated load patterns. Not intended for total datacenter outages or hardware failures—see separate disaster/runbooks. Assumptions and prerequisites ----------------------------- - Observability: per-tenant metrics ingested into telemetry pipeline (token_rps, tokens_per_second, active_sessions, cache_hit_ratio, queue_length, latencies p50/p90/p99, gpu_utilization). - Rate-limiter and quota enforcement via tenant admission controller. - Operator role with access to operator CLI and limited control-plane APIs. - Runbook-tested canary and rollback automation available in the operator toolkit. Key concepts and rationale ------------------------- 1) Burst absorber: a time-limited buffer layer and soft-throttles that let transient spikes be absorbed without immediate full eviction of tenant work. This is implemented by: - short-lived queuing (max queue time 60s) - adaptive batch size reduction to prioritize latency-sensitive requests - temporary credit-based bump for tenants with stable historical behavior 2) Eviction: a last-resort, surgical eviction of tenant runtime working set (KV entries, prefetched model shards) to reclaim memory/GPU cache. Eviction targets cached artifacts and not persistent customer data. 3) Safety gates: any eviction action requires crossing

autoscaling, routing fallback, or human remediation can prevent termination. All escrow actions are auditable. Runbook: Automated Response Flow -------------------------------- 1) Detection and confirmation (oncall or automation) - Verify signals (SLO dashboards and raw metrics). If alert correlates with queue.wait_time.p95 and gpu.utilization > 85%, treat as confirmed. 2) Soft governor (automatic) - throttle-governor applies slice-level rate reductions: reduce best-effort to 40% of baseline, standard to 75%, premium unchanged. - Update oracle: post a change event to /events/capacity-governor with reason and change-id. 3) Escalation and escrow (conditional) - If soft governor does not restore SLOs in 10m, enter escrow evaluation. - Candidate selection heuristic: tenants with highest recent error-budget-burn and lowest contract-priority are shortlisted. - Place shortlisted tenants into eviction escrow with TTL=10min. Notify tenant owners via email/webhook and record in audit log: audit.eviction_escrow.<change-id>. 4) Forced eviction (manual or automated) - After TTL, if no remediation (autoscale or re-route), execute eviction handler to free nodes. Evictions should prefer ephemeral, non-critical worker pods first. - For each eviction, emit events, update chargeback ledger, and annotate tenant with eviction_reason and remediation_instructions. 5) Recovery and soft-restoration - Gradually revert governor reductions in 5-minute increments while monitoring SLOs. Runbook: Manual Intervention Steps ---------------------------------- 1) Triage (first 10 minutes) - Confirm cluster-level telemetry and cross-check tenant logs. - Run quick capacity audit: kubectl get nodes (filter: inference-enabled), check gpu health and pod eviction counts. 2) Apply targeted throttles (if automation disabled) - CLI: curl -X POST https://throttle-api.internal/v1/slices/adjust -d '{"slice":"best-effort","multiplier":0.4}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer $SRE_TOKEN' 3) Place or remove

Progressive Degradation and Tenant Throttling Playbook Summary:
This playbook describes the recommended patterns, operator procedures, and automated controls for progressive degradation and tenant-level throttling in private (VPC/on‑prem) Redwood deployments. It provides a step-by-step runbook for safely limiting tenant resource consumption while maintaining the best possible service for remaining traffic. The goal is to keep high-priority requests healthy, preserve KV/LLM cache integrity where possible, and provide clear operator actions and rollback paths.

Scope and intent:
- Applies to private deployments (VPC and on‑prem control planes) running multi‑tenant inference nodes or shared service planes.
- Focus on non-destructive throttling (rate limits, concurrency caps, queueing and shed patterns) and progressive feature degradation (smaller model fallbacks, quantized execution, disabled non-critical features).
- Designed for both reactive incident response and pre-emptive autoscale-driven protective behaviors.

Key definitions:
- Tenant: customer namespace, logical tenant on the control plane.
- Progressive degradation: ordered, reversible reduction of functionality (e.g., disable long-context mode, reduce max_tokens) to reduce resource pressure.
- Throttling: controls limiting request rate, concurrency, token throughput.
- SLOs referenced: 99th percentile tail latency (p99), request success rate, and model correctness (measured by quality guards).

High-level strategy:
1) Detect: use telemetry to identify high-usage tenants or runaway traffic patterns.
2) Contain: apply per-tenant soft limits and backpressure to stop immediate pressure on shared resources.
3) Degrade progressively: move the tenant through an ordered set of fallbacks that trade capabilities for resource savings.
4) Observe: confirm reduction in pressure and validate critical customer flows remain functional.
5) Restore: rollback degradations in controlled stages after pressure normalizes.

- Metrics: tenant_request_rate, tenant_concurrent_sessions, tenant_tokens_per_minute, node_gpu_utilization_5m, kv_cache_hit_rate, p99_response_ms,

Probabilistic SLO Headroom and Tenancy Reconciliation Playbook Overview Purpose: This playbook codifies a probabilistic, tenant-aware approach to SLO headroom calculation and reconciliation. It is intended for SREs and platform engineers responsible for multi-tenant inference capacity planning, incident response where SLO degradation is capacity-driven, and post-incident forensic analysis. Scope: Applies to Redwood hosted and Dedicated inference services (model-serving clusters) where tenants are logically isolated but share heterogeneous GPU pools. Does not replace contractual capacity commitments for Dedicated customers; it augments them with probabilistic signals that improve runtime resilience for shared clusters. Why this exists Traditional static headroom targets (e.g., keep 20% spare capacity) do not capture burstiness in inference workloads or correlated tenant spikes. We instead model headroom probabilistically from tenant-level usage distributions and SLO expenditure traces, and provide concrete reconciliation steps when SLOs degrade. This reduces unnecessary overprovisioning while preserving customer-facing reliability. Key concepts and definitions - Headroom: the capacity margin expressed as a probability that the cluster can absorb an additional X RPS for Y minutes without breaching p99 latency SLO. - Burn profile: time-series of SLO error budget consumption per tenant and per model route. - Tenancy risk score: composite score for each tenant computed from burst factor, historical variance, contractual tier, and active change events. - Admission controller: runtime gate that admits or rejects requests when capacity budget threatens SLOs. - Soft eviction: non-destructive mitigation that reduces tenant concurrency or reroutes to lower-cost model variants. - Hard eviction: temporary suspension of non-critical tenant traffic (last resort). Tenant entropy, stability, and runtime safeguards Overview Purpose: This playbook defines pragmatic safeguards, operational controls, and runbook procedures to manage tenant-level entropy (unpredictable resource usage, thermal events, KV cache churn, and noisy neighbors) in private VPC and on-prem Redwood deployments. The goal is to preserve tenant SLAs while providing clear escalation, telemetry, and rollback actions for field operators. Scope: applies to Private (VPC and on-prem) deployments running the Redwood runtime (all supported versions) and to operator teams responsible for tenant onboarding, capacity zoning, and steady-state ops. Audience: SRE/Field Ops, Private Deploy Customer Engineers, Platform Reliability, and Solutions Engineering. Key concepts and definitions - Tenant entropy: any sudden or non-linear divergence in a tenant's resource or behavioral profile (examples: bursty seq-length distributions, KV cache thrash, high-attention memory growth due to long-context requests). - Containment: automated or manual actions that limit blast radius (rate limiting, synthetic throttles, eviction, tenant quarantine). - Soft vs hard fallback: soft falls redirect to compatible model variants or reduced batch sizes; hard falls stop new sessions to protect cluster core functions. SLOs and operational thresholds - Per-tenant P99 latency SLO for interactive endpoints: 95% of tenants remain below 750ms P99 under normal load. - System-wide total GPU utilization target: 55-85% steady state; sustained >90% triggers containment flow. - KV cache hit rate guardrail: for production tenants, maintain >65% prefix hit rate; a sustained drop >20ppts for >10 minutes should trigger investigation. - Thermal margin: GPU temperature > 78C sustained for 2 minutes -> schedule immediate workload shedding

SLO harmonization and progressive throttling handbook: tenant fairness & burst variance Summary:
This handbook defines a cross-service approach for harmonizing SLOs across heterogeneous inference workloads, handling burst variance without destabilizing the fleet, and implementing a progressive throttling controller that enforces tenant fairness. It combines capacity budgeting, proportional error-budget gating, and a gradual throttling algorithm to preserve critical customer SLOs while preventing noisy-neighbor cascades.

Intended audience:
- SREs and Platform Engineers responsible for multi-tenant capacity
- Oncall responders handling SLO regressions and throttling events
- Product and Customer Reliability partners who negotiate SLO contracts

Goals:
- Provide a repeatable process for aligning individual service SLOs with global capacity constraints
- Ensure predictable, auditable throttling decisions with tenant fairness guarantees
- Reduce incident surface caused by bursty tenants while limiting user-visible degradation

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to Redwood public-hosted inference endpoints, Dedicated pools, and Private VPC routable clusters (where platform-level throttling exists)
- Focus on multi-tenant GPU-backed text generation and embedding workloads with token-based billing
- Not intended for single-tenant Dedicated reservations or external partner on-prem appliances that enforce customer-managed throttles

Definitions and primitives:

- Error budget: The remaining allowable fraction of user-facing failure within the SLO window. Error budget spend drives remediation urgency and rollback decisions.
- Triage window: 30 minutes for initial assessment, 2 hours for stabilization plan, 24 hours for remediation plan.

SLO arbitration canvas and scripting cookbook Overview Purpose: This document defines the SLO arbitration canvas — a lightweight decision framework and accompanying operator scripting cookbook for platform operators to make deterministic choices when multiple SLOs conflict during capacity shortages, model cascades, or regional degradations. The goal is to make trade-offs repeatable, auditable, and automatable. Who should use this doc: - Platform operators running regional operator consoles - Oncall engineers executing mitigation steps during degradation - Platform product owners designing graceful degradation policies Background and motivation: Redwood's multi-tenant inference surface exposes numerous SLOs simultaneously (tail latency, p50 token latency for interactive customers, throughput for batch customers, token-cost SLOs for internal billing cadence, and quality regressions for model variants). Historically, operators relied on ad-hoc judgement when arbitrary combinations of alerts fired. That led to inconsistent customer impact and avoidable cost. The arbitration canvas reduces cognitive load by enumerating priority axes, safe fallbacks, and deterministic scriptable actions. Key definitions: - SLI: observable metric (e.g., delivery.latency_99, generate.tokens_per_second). - SLO: target over rolling window (e.g., delivery.latency_99 < 200ms over 1h). - Arbitration policy: ordered rules mapping SLO breach contexts -> action sets. - Action set: set of operator-invokable steps (scripts, API calls, manual checks). High-level arbitration flow (summary): 1) Ingest signals: SLO breach alarms + contextual telemetry (tenant, model, region, queue depth). 2) Classify scenario: use deterministic matcher to map to scenario type (Capacity Scarcity, Model Misbehaviour, Regional Network Degradation, Cost Spike). 3) Evaluate policy matrix: apply prioritized rules to select a candidate action set.

This page documents the Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net design pattern, associated capacity planning guidance, operational tooling integrations, and an actionable SRE runbook for managing high-consumption error budgets across multi-tenant inference services. The pattern is intended to reduce blast radius, keep critical customers online, and defer costly capacity purchases while enforcing reliability commitments.

Scope and audience:
- SREs responsible for inference-serving SLOs and multi-tenant capacity governance
- Platform/product owners defining SLO contracts for tenants
- Incident commanders and oncall engineers who execute capacity and throttling actions

Problem statement:
As inference workloads become more heterogeneous, single-threshold error-budget triggers either overreact (unnecessary capacity spend) or underreact (missed mitigations). A tiered safety-net provides graduated mitigations mapped to business impact and tenancy class.

 - Advisory (>=30% consumed): notifications, suggested knob recommendations, additional telemetry collection.
 - Protective (>=70% consumed): soft preemption of lowest-priority requests, enable conservative batching heuristics, spin up elastic reserved nodes.
 - Emergency (>=100% consumed or sustained

allocating-burn-and-recovery-runbook-for-heterogeneous-inference-workloads Overview: This runbook describes a standardized process for allocating, redistributing, and recovering SLO error budget across heterogeneous inference workloads (text generation, embeddings, ranking) in Redwood's multi-tenant serving environment. It captures operational rules, telemetry signals, and step-by-step procedures SREs should follow when multiple services are consuming shared capacity and a centralized error-budget pool requires reconciliation. The goal is to preserve customer-facing latency and availability SLOs while minimizing cost and avoiding unnecessary tenant evictions. Scope: - Applies to: hosted-api and dedicated clusters where multiple tenants (internal and external) share inference capacity under a common autoscaling/priority controller. - NOT in scope: fully isolated Private on-prem clusters with per-customer reserved-only capacity. Definitions and concepts: 1) Error budget: The allowable SLO burn for a given service over a rolling window (default 28d) measured as error-rate (availability) and latency tail (p99/p999). 2) Centralized burn pool: A computed view of aggregate budget consumption across a logical capacity pool used for short-term redistribution and emergency hedging. 3) Hedging capacity: Pre-authorized spare capacity allocated to absorb transient surges without triggering tenant throttles. 4) Fractional redistribution: Temporarily reweighting error budget shares across tenants when one tenant's workload causes disproportionate burn. Principles: - Preserve user-facing availability first. Latency SLOs may degrade in controlled, observable ways if availability is at risk. - Prefer graduated, reversible actions (rate-limits, soft degrades, model variant fallbacks) over hard evictions. - All redistributions must be auditable, timeboxed, and subject to post-action review. - Metric-driven decisions: follow telemetry thresholds and automated scoring for consistency. Service stewardship lifecycle (process overview):
1) Define SLOs and objectives during service onboarding (see SLO template below).
2) Publish error-budget policy: what to do at 50%, 25%, 10%, 0% remaining.
3) Maintain capacity runway >= 14 days under expected growth OR implement automated admission controls.
4) Run monthly stewardship review: verify dashboards, runbook accuracy, and on-call readiness.
5) After any Critical degradation: open a post-incident review, create capacity remediation tickets, and follow the slice-and-fix cadence in this doc.

Error budget guardrail policy (standard template):
- Measurement window: 30-day rolling by default. Some critical services (payment, auth) use 7-day rolling.
- Threshold actions:
 - >= 50% budget remaining: normal operations; steward monitors burn rate weekly.
 - >= 25% and < 50%: steward must notify product and SRE; schedule capacity forecast within 48 hours.
 - >= 10% and < 25%: steward triggers a targeted mitigation plan (rate limit non-essential traffic, enable caching layers, temporarily reduce batch sizes to reduce CPU).
 - < 10%: automatic admission-controller shifts to conservative mode; throttle new low-priority tokens by 30% and open urgent capacity ticket.
 - 0%: emergency degrade plan: non-critical features disabled, reserve capacity pool engaged, and SRE leads incident exec until recovery.

Automated enforcement actions (examples):
- Admission controller policy: when error budget < 10%, apply annotation on service to route new requests through conservative path (config: admission-policy=conservative).
- Cache warming and prefix KV restore: run warming job to prime frequently used KV segments on recovery.
- Canary throttles: route 5% of traffic to fallback model until

budget to recover (e.g., 30m). - Amortization Staircase: ordered fidelity steps applied at deterministic intervals. - Safety Gate: quality and latency checks that must pass before launching the next step up. ADR-0143: Error Budget Burn-Rate Alerting Approach (Multi-window) ## Summary We will use **multi-window error-budget burn-rate alerting** (Google SRE-style) as the canonical alerting approach for tiered SLOs (Hosted vs Dedicated). Alerts will be computed from the same SLIs that drive SLO reporting and error budget accounting. This ADR defines: - How we compute burn rate (relative to a tier’s SLO) - Standard alert window pairs and thresholds for paging vs ticketing - Guardrails (minimum traffic, missing data behavior) - Trade-offs vs static threshold alerting (e.g., “5xx > 1%”) ## Status **Accepted** and implemented as the default for tiered SLO alerting starting Q1 2026 rollout (warn-only enforcement phase). ## Context / Problem Redwood Inference is formalizing tiered SLOs and an enforced error budget policy. We need an alerting strategy that: - **Aligns directly** with customer-facing reliability commitments (SLOs) across tiers - Detects both **fast-burning incidents** (regressions, regional failures) and **slow burns** (capacity drift, noisy neighbor issues) - Scales across endpoint classes (chat/completions, embeddings, streaming) and regions without excessive manual tuning - Avoids noisy alerts from short-lived blips that don’t meaningfully impact SLO attainment Historically, we relied on static alerts like “HTTP 5xx rate > X% for Y minutes” and “p95 latency > Z ms.” These alerts: - Do not map cleanly to tiered SLOs (Hosted vs Dedicated have different targets) - Encourage threshold debates rather than focusing on error budget impact - Can be simultaneously too noisy (small transient spikes) and too slow (gradual burn never crosses a hard threshold) ## Decision

Signals and metrics - Primary signals (required): - request_success_rate (rolling 5m, 1h, 24h) - p99_latency_ms (90d baseline) - queue_depth and eviction_rate for inference workers - capacity_utilization (GPU/CPU) per pool - Secondary signals (optional): - model_kv_cache_miss_rate - cold_start_rate for worker pods - error_type breakdown (5xx, 429, pattern matches) Mapping: EB state -> automated actions (default orchestration policy) - EB burn rate < 3x (GREEN): no automatic mitigation. Capacity fuzzy hedging and error-bank playbook Overview ======= This playbook defines the 'fuzzy hedging' approach to capacity and a complementary operational pattern we call the Error Bank: a short-term, auditable tokenized buffer that lets teams absorb transient SLO consumption spikes without immediate full-capacity commitments. The goal is to improve customer-facing reliability while minimizing costly overprovisioning and preserving clear recovery paths. Key outcomes: - Reduce unnecessary reserved capacity spend by 10–35% for bursty tenants. - Keep P99 latency SLOs intact for customer-critical tiers during short-term load spikes. - Provide rapid, low-friction mitigation options for oncall with clear revert criteria. When to use this playbook ------------------------ - For multi-tenant inference services with bursty or seasonal traffic (embedding jobs, batch reranking, real-time spikes). - When rapid headroom provisioning takes >10 minutes or carries a significant cost commitment. - As an intermediate mitigation layer between autoscaling and tenant throttling/eviction. Core concepts ------------- 1) Fuzzy hedging (probabilistic headroom allocation) - Use probabilistic forecasts (mix of short-term EWMA and calendar-aware ML model) to allocate ephemeral headroom instead of hard slot reservations. - Hedge factor (H) is defined per-tenant-class: H = quantile(forecast, q) * safety_multiplier. Typical defaults: q=0.90 for standard tenants, q=0.98 for enterprise-critical. safety_multiplier in [1.05, 1.20]. 2) Error Bank (tokenized short-term error-credit) - Error Bank is a per-tenant credit account expressed in SLO-seconds (e.g., latency or error budget units) that can be consumed automatically under controlled conditions. - Bank top-ups are policy-driven (manual, scheduled, or earned via low-burn windows). 3) Tiered fallback policy - Tier

windows - Primary window: **28 days** - Secondary windows: 7 days, 1 day (for fast detection) ### What consumes budget A minute consumes budget when all of the following are true: - Volume gate is met (see below) - Telemetry quality is healthy (no pipeline drop indicators) - Guardrail threshold is violated (relative to baseline or vs control) ### Budget actions - >80% remaining: no action (observe) - 50–80% remaining: file investigation ticket to Runtime/Platform (non-urgent) - 20–50% remaining: escalate to oncall lead for prioritization in sprint - <20% remaining: declare reliability initiative and schedule remediation (may include config changes, routing policy adjustments, cache sizing) Note: We do not want the “budget” to imply customer SLO compliance; it is used to prioritize engineering work. ## Alerting proposal (page vs ticket) ### Alert classes 1) **Page (P1/P2) only for likely systemic regressions** Page criteria (must meet all): - Sustained violation (multi-window) AND - High confidence signal (volume gate + telemetry healthy) AND - Strong indicator of platform regression (miss_reason spike in policy_disabled/version_mismatch, or near-zero hit rate with high eligibility) 2) **Ticket (P3) for slow burns / optimization opportunities** - Relative regressions without clear systemic cause - Wasted prefill increase without latency impact - Elevated eviction pressure correlated with specific model/region 3) **Noisy/anomalous (auto-silence)** - Low volume - Known maintenance windows - Known workload migration events (route moved, model rollout in progress) unless canary/control comparison indicates a true regression ### Initial alert rules (recommended) These are expressed as intent; implementation may vary

For every SLO we track a percentage of budget consumed per window. - DEB maintains a separate budget for: latency, availability, correctness/quality. We normalize to percent remaining. - For Latency budget: compute fraction of requests that violated latency threshold over the window; budget_remaining = 1 - violation_fraction. - For Correctness budget: use regression test failure fraction on sampled checks. Pause non-essential background jobs, enable aggressive autoscale, reduce tenant burst allowances, start capacity hedging. - Red (<10% remaining) — emergency. Key concepts - Capacity floor: guaranteed baseline vGPU/slice per tenant (steady-state allocation). - Burst credit: a consumable budget (measured in GPU-credit-seconds) that lets a tenant exceed their floor for limited time. - Replenishment window: rolling 24-hour window when credits regenerate. - Throttle policy: ordered fallback actions when credits are exhausted (soft-degrade -> model fallback -> queuing -> hard-throttle). - Fleet reservoir: an emergency global pool used for critical tenants or safety net during partial outages. Design: credit accounting and formulas 1) Units: GPU-credit-seconds (GCS). 1 GCS = 1 GPU * 1 second at baseline utilization. We normalize multi-GPU instances and fractional multiplexing into equivalent GCS. 2) Baseline allocation: each tenant has an allocated baseline B (GCS/sec). Typical baseline examples: 0.05 GCS/s (light), 0.5 GCS/s (medium), 2.0 GCS/s (heavy). 3) Credit pool size (P) formula: P = min(MAX_POOL, floor_multiplier * B * REPLENISH_WINDOW_SECONDS) Where: - floor_multiplier = default 6 (configurable by tenant tier) - REPLENISH_WINDOW_SECONDS = 24 * 3600 = 86_400 - MAX_POOL = 1_000_000 GCS (global per-tenant cap) 4) Consumption during burst: consumed = sum_over_time((consumed_gpus(t) - B) * delta_t) for consumed_gpus > B 5) Soft recovery: if consumed < B, credits are replenished at a configurable reclaim rate (default 1.0x real-time up to the pool cap). GPU burst shock-absorber: Terraform operator design and safety specification Overview

This page defines the design, Terraform operator contract, CI/CD gating, and runbook for the GPU Burst Shock-Absorber (GBSA) — an infrastructure component that protects tenant-facing inference services from capacity shocks by absorbing, smoothing, and rate-limiting burst demand across heterogeneous GPU pools. It is an operator + Terraform pattern intended for use in Dedicated and Private deployment modes where cost, latency SLOs, and tenant isolation must be balanced.

Goals

- Provide a predictable, SLO-aware buffer that: absorbs sudden tenant bursts; avoids mass preemptions; and provides graceful degradation tiers.
- Expose a declarative Terraform resource that teams can include in their tenant stacks (self-serve) to opt into burst protection.
- Ensure safety by default: automated canaries, rate-limit leashing, and multi-stage rollback behaviors.
- Operate compatibly with existing chargeback, billing, and telemetry pipelines.

Non-goals

- GBSA will not replace long-term capacity planning or tenant quotas. It is a short-term shock-mitigation mechanism (minutes to hours).
- It is not a tenant-level autoscaler — it smooths bursts rather than permanently provisioning new quota.

High-level architecture

1) Control plane (operator): runs as a Kubernetes operator in the infra control cluster. Responsibilities: reconcile GBSA custom resources (CRs), orchestrate allocation handoffs, perform pre-checks with Terraform state, and emit telemetry events.
2) Bridge module (Terraform): a declarative module that registers tenant intent, attaches policies (SLO thresholds, billing caps), and emits a CRD manifest the operator will reconcile.
3) Runtime adapters: small platform services that implement the actual runtime behavior — a rate limiter service, a KV cache seeder, and a pool-allocator shim

policy: Changes to the gpu_pool module require a TF plan published in CI and a manual approval for production changes.
- Canary rollout steps for topology/affinity changes (automated pipeline):
 1. Create a canary pool with identical module inputs but capacity_target = 5% of desired final size and label canary=true.
 2. Run integration tests: placement latency, preemption simulation, network egress test.
 3. Promote canary: gradually increase capacity in 3 steps (5% -> 25% -> 100%) with 30-minute observation windows.
 4. If any critical metric crosses thresholds (see "Safety thresholds" below), rollback via terraform apply to previous module state.

Safety thresholds:
- placement.fallback_rate > 2% for 10 continuous minutes -> pause rollout and scale up warm pool
- pool.preemptions_per_minute spike to > 0.5% of pool.size -> pause canary and notify SRE
- network.egress_errors_rate > 0.2% -> rollback egress policy change

1. Verify demand trend in dashboard and cross-check cost impact in billing dashboard.
2. Create TF change for pool capacity_target delta. Run CI plan and ensure no other pending changes.
3. Apply to staging/canary pools first and observe 2x placement latency and headroom for 2 hours.
4. Apply to production pools during a low-traffic window (if possible) and monitor. Notify oncall via Slack channel #infra-gpu.

The goal is to provide clear, predictable behavior when capacity, cost, or external dependency issues require graceful reduction in delivered fidelity. Non-goals: - ASDL is not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or for manual contractual SLA negotiation. - It does not replace model-quality guardrails: model regressions should be surfaced by evals and rollback pipelines. evaluation_chunks.content: Cascading SLO Failure Mitigation and Federated Budget Playbook Summary: This playbook defines a federated SLO budget model and an operational runbook to detect, contain, and recover from cascading SLO failures across the Redwood inference stack (edge proxy, routing, serving runtime, and storage/KV subsystems). It prescribes an automated credit-leasing protocol, priority-driven request shaping, and manual escalation steps to preserve critical SLAs while minimizing customer impact and cost. Scope: - Applies to: edge-proxy, request-router, runtime-allocator, kv-cache, model-serving pool (hosted and dedicated), and routing fallback orchestrator. - Not in scope: billing reconciliation, model training pipelines, and customer-managed on-prem control planes (except where telemetry proxies route to Redwood control plane). Motivation: Cascading failures often occur when one subsystem exhausts its capacity and backpressure is incorrectly propagated or unbounded. We need a bounded, auditable mechanism to reallocate limited SLO budget across services and tenants in a predictable way and an operational checklist for engineers and on-call to act quickly. Definitions: - Federated SLO Budget: a per-service pool of SLO 'credits' (latency/error allowances) that can be temporarily leased to dependent services during transient pressure. - Credit Lease: a time-bound transfer of budget from one service's pool to another with automatic repayment rules. - Priority Lane: a request classification (critical/standard/batch) used to drive admission control and shaping. - Degradation Fence: pre-approved behavior that reduces fidelity (quantization, token limit, sampling) for non-critical traffic. Design Principles: - Predictability: leases are capped, time-limited, and compensated in repayment windows to avoid permanent budget erosion. - Observability-first: every lease, shape, and eviction

Contain token cost increase for unaffected tenants to <= 10% during mitigation windows. Principles 1. Fast detection — prioritize cheap, high-signal telemetry (kernel queue latency, GPU utilization spikes, KV cache miss-rate) for initial decisioning. 2. Graceful degradation — step down fidelity in controlled stages (e.g., quantized variant, smaller context window, prefix cache warmup) instead of abrupt circuit breakers. 3. Isolation by policy — prefer routing heuristics and tenant-weighted admission controls over full-host quarantine where possible. 4. Observable and reversible — every fallback must emit a decision trace and be reversible via automatic rollback or manual operator action. Key components and service names - runtime-scheduler: admission control, slot allocation, kernel hint emitter. - kernel-agent: per-GPU kernel selector / binder and health checker. - kvcache-manager: prefix KV cache owner, warmup controller. - fallback-router: policy engine to reroute requests to alternative variants/regions. - telemetry-pipeline: high-frequency telemetry ingestion and decision-triggering alerts. Decision graph (high level) 1) Detect anomaly — telemetry-pipeline raises condition (e.g., node_kernel_timeout_rate > 0.5% over 1m). 2) Evaluate impact window — runtime-scheduler queries kvcache-manager and kernel-agent for eviction rates and kernel latencies. 3) Apply kinetic fallback Stage A (non-disruptive): increase per-tenant slot circuit cap, enable local KV cache aggressive rewarm, issue kernel preference hints (prefer fused-kernel-lite). 4) If condition persists, Stage B (fidelity reduction): fallback-router switches non-critical tenants to quantized model_variant-q8 and reduces max-generation-length to 512 tokens. 5) Stage C (isolation): runtime-scheduler enacts tenant-weighted throttling and migrates hot tenants off the degraded node. 6) Recovery: reverse stages in order; verify telemetry returns

ADR: SLO federation and weighted degradation policy Overview This ADR establishes a federated SLO model and a weighted degradation policy for the inference runtime and adjacent services. The goal is to provide clear, predictable behavior when capacity, cost, or external dependency issues require graceful reduction in delivered fidelity. Motivation - Historically, service-level objectives (SLOs) at Redwood have been defined per-service with hard failover rules. This produced brittle user experiences when multi-service requests (for example: routing, KV cache, model variant selection) disagreed on priorities. - Customers require both predictable latency and predictable token-unit costs. A single hard-fail SLO does not express trade-offs between cost, latency, and output fidelity. - We need an orchestrated, auditable way to reduce output fidelity with minimal user-facing downtime while honoring contractual SLAs (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Decision We adopt a federated SLO model plus a lightweight weighted-degradation policy: 1) SLO federation - Each logical request path composes SLOs from participating services (edge-proxy, routing, runtime, KV-cache, model-store). - Composition rule: compute a weighted SLO score where each service contributes a normalized metric (p99 latency, error-rate, cost-per-token) with a configured weight. The top-level SLO is the aggregation of these weighted scores. - Ownership: each service owns its local SLI definitions and the weight it contributes to federation (default weights stored in /service-config/slo-weights). 2) Weighted degradation policy - When the federated SLO breaches a configured threshold, the system triggers a graded degradation controller (GDC). The GDC reduces fidelity according to a ranked list of degradation steps with associated

Crossplane fallback & profiling playbook: diagnosing fused fallbacks across scheduler layers Summary ------- This playbook documents how to diagnose, triage, and remediate cross-layer fallback events in the serving runtime when the router, kernel-dispatcher, and kv-cache layers interact to trigger graceful degradations. It focuses on a class of incidents we call 'fused fallbacks' — when multiple subsystems independently activate fallback policies and the system degrades more than intended (e.g., model swap + kernel downgrade + cache eviction). Audience -------- - Oncall SREs and runtime engineers handling production incidents. - Performance engineers running microbenchmarks and regression hunts. - Release engineers validating canaries for new scheduler or kernel rollouts. Why this is different -------------------- Existing runbooks cover single-layer fallback (router or kernel) or warmstart strategies. This document covers the combined behavioral surface: how fallback signals propagate, what telemetry to collect to see the causal chain, and an ordered mitigation sequence that minimizes user-visible SLO impact. Key goals and SLOs ------------------ - SLOs to use during triage: p50 < 60ms, p95 < 220ms, p99 < 700ms for short-text generation (seq<=128) on hosted tier. - Fallback budget: total degraded token-rate should be <5% of baseline over 5m rolling window. - Alert thresholds: sustained 2x increase in kernel-handled-slow-calls with concurrent model-variant-swaps > 10/min. Primary services and signals to inspect ------------------------------------- - inference-router: routing decisions, chosen-tier, model-variant-id, timestamped route decisions (field: route_decision.trace_id). - kernel-dispatcher: kernel_version, queue_depth, dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_error_rate. - kv-cache-manager: hit_rate, warmup_ratio, eviction_rate, per-tenant cache_size_bytes. - fallthrough-agent: fused-fallback-events log (proto), reason codes (NETWORK_PRESSURE, KERNEL_TIMEOUT, CACHE_WARMUP_FAIL). - telemetry-ingester

SLO taxonomy, capacity smoothing, and graceful degradation playbook Summary This playbook defines a practical SLO taxonomy, links error budgets to capacity smoothing policies, and prescribes a standardized runbook for planned and emergency graceful degradation. It is intended for service owners, SREs, and platform engineers responsible for production model-serving and user-facing features. Why this exists - SLOs need to map cleanly to capacity decisions and automated traffic shaping. - Error budgets should drive predictable, transparent throttling and fallbacks—not ad-hoc firefighting. - Teams must have a shared, low-friction procedure to degrade features while preserving critical SLAs. Scope - Applies to all public and internal Redwood inference endpoints and associated control planes. - Focuses on latency and availability SLOs for tokenized inferencing, plus success-rate SLOs for control APIs (model selection, rollouts). - Excludes long-term architectural work (e.g., major re-architectures), which should use the ADR process. SLO taxonomy (recommended) 1) Latency SLOs (user-facing generation paths) - p95 and p99 completion latency measured at the API gateway post-auth. - Example: "generation.p95 < 250ms" (for interactive endpoints) 2) Availability SLOs (API success rate) - Rolling 30d window success rate (2xx responses / total non-retryable requests). - Example: "generation.success >= 99.9% (30d)" 3) Quality SLOs (internal, tied to evals) - Periodic prompt set regression thresholds; tracked but not used for automated throttling. 4) Control-plane SLOs - Model rollout operations: apply/rollback must succeed within 5 minutes 99% of the time. Mapping SLOs to Error Budgets - Error budget = 1 - SLO. Reserve explicit sub-budgets per consumer type

Cross-tenant failure domain mitigation and kinetic fallback patterns Summary This document defines operational patterns, scheduling knobs, profiling and benchmarking steps for mitigating cross-tenant failure domains and implementing kinetic fallback behaviors in the runtime. It consolidates architecture intent, kernel scheduling recommendations, specific runbooks for incidents, and a minimal benchmarking protocol to validate mitigations before rollout. Audience - Runtime engineers (kernel and scheduler owners) - SREs who operate GPU pools and admission controllers - Platform product managers planning fallbacks and SLAs Context and problem statement Cross-tenant failure domains occur when a fault (hardware, thermal, driver, model regression, or noisy neighbor) degrades quality-of-service for multiple tenants sharing a GPU node, a rack, or a scheduler queue. Without explicit mitigation, symptoms include elevated p95/p99 latency, KV-cache churn, kernel timeouts, and degraded throughput. Traditional single-tenant isolation strategies are expensive; instead we use kinetic fallback patterns — adaptive, fast-acting fallbacks that proactively reduce fidelity or change routing to preserve SLOs for unaffected tenants while isolating failure impact. Goals and SLOs - Preserve tenant-facing availability: 99.95% uptime per customer pool (monthly). - Maintain latency SLOs under degraded conditions: p95 <= 60ms, p99 <= 200ms for standard generation routes; critical routes p95 <= 40ms, p99 <= 120ms. - Contain token cost increase for unaffected tenants to <= 10% during mitigation windows. Adaptive SLO Shepherding & Capacity Fencing Playbook Overview This playbook codifies an adaptive approach we call "SLO shepherding" for day-to-day SRE operations: proactively protecting critical SLOs by applying capacity fencing, tenant reservations, and temporary degradation policies while preserving error-budget fairness across tenants. It combines measurement, automated tooling, and human guardrails to avoid surprise outages and prevent long reconciliations after incidents. Scope & applicability - Applies to multi-tenant inference services: inference-gateway, model-host-pool, and routing-proxy. - Intended for services with latency or availability SLOs and where capacity is a constrained resource (GPU pools, KV cache memory, or token throughput). - Not intended for non-production dev environments or single-tenant dedicated customers (those use dedicated capacity contracts). Goals 1. Keep critical customer-facing SLOs within target (example target: 99.95% availability monthly; p99 latency < 350ms for small text-gen). 2. Avoid global emergency scaling that undermines fairness: use fenced capacity to protect tiered SLAs. 3. Provide clear, repeatable runbooks for Capacity Fencing events and Post-Incident Review evidence. Key service SLOs (examples) | Service | SLO (primary) | Window | Alert threshold | |---|---:|---:|---:| | inference-gateway | p99 latency < 350ms | 30d rolling | p99 > 350ms for 30m | | model-host-pool | request success rate >= 99.95% | 30d rolling | 1h error rate > 0.5% | | routing-proxy | availability >= 99.9% | 30d rolling | 15m availability < 99% | Error budget policy summary - Error budget = 1 - SLO. Consumption is measured at the service-level per 30-day window. - Progressive response

reclaim action on a worker; fallback is a traffic-routing reaction at the decision layer. SLO thresholds and mapping (operational values): - Availability SLO: 99.9% over 30 days. - Latency SLOs: p50 <= 50ms; p95 <= 120ms; p99 <= 320ms for short-chat routes (<=256 tokens). Long-form routes have route-specific p99s. - Fallback trigger thresholds (examples): - p99 observed > 1.5x configured SLO for five consecutive 1-minute windows -> candidate fallback. - Error rate (5xx) spike > 3x baseline for 3 consecutive windows -> immediate evaluation. - GPU kernel queue depth > 85% for sustained 30s -> trigger conservative admission. Fallback decision flow (high-level): 1) Detect anomaly: telemetry alert fires (latency/error/queue depth). 2) Correlate signals: match trace ids, kernel-level metrics (kernel latency, occupancy), and recent config changes. 3) Classify cause: kernel regression, model artifact, traffic surge, network degradation, or hardware failure. 4) Action selection: pick from the fallback catalog (model variant swap, route-level throttling, regional reroute, or degrade features). 5) Apply fallback with canary: route 5% -> fallback for 60s, observe p99 and error delta. 6) If successful: gradually ramp to 100% over 10 minutes. 7) If unsuccessful: rollback and escalate to incident channel. Decision heuristics (rules of thumb): - Prefer model-variant fallback when kernel CPU/GPU stalls or kernel timeout errors are observed. - Prefer region-level reroute when network egress/ingress errors are correlated to region telemetry. - Avoid functional-degrading fallbacks (e.g., remove tool-calls) for routes marked "high-fidelity" unless explicitly approved by product. - Maintain conservative prefactors: use 1.5x–2x thresholds for latency-based fallbacks

Adaptive Service Degradation Lattice Spec Summary: This design specification defines the Adaptive Service Degradation Lattice (ASDL), a policy-driven runtime component that enables predictable, auditable, and reversible feature degradations to preserve customer-facing SLOs during resource constraints, regional outages, or degraded model performance. ASDL formalizes a lattice of degradation states, a compact policy language for expressing transitions, telemetry signals for decisioning, and crediting rules to account for customer impact. Why we need it: - We must maintain latency and availability SLOs for paying customers while minimizing revenue and quality regressions across model variants and deployment modes (hosted, dedicated, private). - Current ad-hoc fallbacks (per-service scripts, hardcoded thresholds) create inconsistent customer experiences and are hard to reason about in multi-tenant scenarios where routing, quantization, and caching interact. - ASDL provides a declarative, testable, and observable way to apply multi-dimensional degradations (model fidelity, token budget, batching aggressiveness, KV cache TTL) with clear rollback and crediting semantics. Goals: 1) Provide a runtime policy lattice that maps observed signals to deterministic degradation actions. 2) Make degradations reversible, throttled, and timeboxed with automatic rollback when signals recover. 3) Emit structured decision events that feed billing crediting, incident analysis, and customer-facing notifications. 4) Support per-tenant and per-route overrides, with safe defaults for hosted and dedicated customers. Non-goals: - ASDL is not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or for manual contractual SLA negotiation. - It does not replace model-quality guardrails: model regressions should be surfaced by evals and rollback pipelines. Stakeholders and ownership: - Product: owner for policy

Latency-aware Cost Fallback Protocol (LACFP) Design Spec Summary: This design spec defines the Latency-aware Cost Fallback Protocol (LACFP), a server-side policy and lightweight protocol that enables Redwood inference routing to automatically fall back to lower-cost model variants or capacity tiers when latency, cost, or capacity signals indicate it is appropriate. The goal is to preserve user-facing latency SLOs while minimizing incremental cost and providing transparent accounting for customer billing and internal cost centers. Motivation: - Customers require predictable latency for interactive workloads (e.g., chat) but also demand cost efficiency. - Static fallback rules (time-based or simple capacity thresholds) are brittle and cause noisy behavior during transient events. - We need a shared, auditable protocol that: 1) reacts to latency and cost signals in near real-time; 2) guarantees bounded user-impact by enforcing soft/hard fidelity and latency limits; 3) preserves billable attribution and enables credits/discounting when lower-fidelity fallbacks are applied. Design goals (must): - Latency-first: Respect per-route latency SLOs (default 95th pct <= 120ms for token production in interactive endpoints). - Cost-conscious: Prefer lower-cost variants when they do not violate quality or latency objectives. - Transparent accounting: Emit events for every fallback decision with cost delta metadata for billing reconciliation. - Configurable: Support per-tenant and per-route policies with hierarchical inheritance (global -> tenant -> route). Non-goals (out of scope): - Model distillation, model training, or quality-aware model retraining. - Deep content-aware fidelity negotiation (that belongs to the fidelity negotiator PRD). - Full rewrites of the billing system; LACFP only emits metadata consumed

Service degradation policies and API fallback contracts (ADR) Overview This ADR defines a cross-service standard for graceful degradation and API fallback contracts across Redwood Inference. It covers the expected behavior when components experience overload, partial failure, or resource-constrained conditions and prescribes the observable signals, configuration knobs, and rollout steps engineering teams must follow. The goal is to keep customer-facing applications available with predictable degraded semantics and clear operational ownership. Problem statement As model sizes, throughput demands, and multi-tenant traffic patterns grow, we observe three recurring failure modes: 1) Transient capacity pressure causing tail latency spikes. 2) Component-level outages (runner crash, GPU OOM, KV cache miss storm) leading to partial loss of features. 3) Cascading retries between services causing amplification and broad outages. Without a standardized degradation contract teams implement ad-hoc fallbacks: inconsistent HTTP response codes, unclear metrics, and uncontrolled retry behavior. This ADR sets required minimal behavior so upper-layer clients (web, batch, mobile) can implement robust fallbacks and UX teams can design consistent messages. Decision summary We adopt a standardized, implementation-agnostic service degradation contract: - Services expose a prioritized capability set (primary, reduced, degraded) via a /v1/capabilities endpoint and an X-Redwood-Degradation header on responses. - SLO-driven automatic degradation: when tail latency (P99) or error-rate breach configured thresholds, services must flip to a reduced capability mode within 30s and signal the change through metrics and headers. - Fallback policy: consumers must treat 503 + Retry-After as a soft-fail and 200 + degraded payload as acceptable reduced-quality response. - Observability and playbooks:

Service Fidelity, Cost Tradeoffs, and SLO Matrix Framework Overview This document defines a pragmatic framework for reasoning about service fidelity, per-request cost, and SLO placement across Redwood Inference's serving surface. It codifies a matrix for mapping request classes to SLO/budget pairs, prescribes API-level hints to enable runtime cost/fidelity negotiation, and provides an operational rollout and measurement playbook. The goal is to make tradeoffs repeatable, observable, and reversible. Why this exists (Motivation) - Rising model heterogeneity (full-precision, quantized, distilled variants) and multi-modal endpoints demand explicit guidance on when to sacrifice fidelity to save cost. - Customers require predictable unit economics; teams need standard controls for graceful quality degradation under constrained capacity. - Existing standards cover SLOs and fallback but do not specify a cross-cutting mapping from request intent -> fidelity budget -> runtime config. Scope - Applies to all Redwood runtime surfaces: Hosted API, Dedicated pools, and Private deployments. - Targets text generation, chat sessions, and embedding requests. Does not change model artifacts or evaluation standards; it augments serving and API semantics. Definitions - Fidelity tier: qualitative label representing expected output quality (e.g., "high-precision", "balanced", "fast-safe"). - Cost budget: expected token or GPU cost per request (USD/normalized-unit) or a relative multiplier. - Request class: classification of a call by business intent (e.g., transactional, exploratory, background-batch). - Negotiation hint: API-level field that signals client preference along latency/cost/fidelity axes. Principles 1. Observable tradeoffs: Every degradation must have an associated metric (quality SLI) and cost delta. 2. Testable fallbacks: Fallback variants must be regression-tested

Latency Budgeting and Decisive Fallback Canvas Overview This page defines a compact, operator-friendly canvas for latency budgeting across LLM inference stacks and a decisive fallback matrix to keep customer-facing routes within SLOs during transient or sustained degradation. The goal is to give oncall and platform operators a single reference that ties SLO targets, dashboard signals, alerts, immediate mitigation steps, longer-term remediation, and roadmap work into one actionable artifact. During oncall when a latency SLO is burning and the root cause is uncertain. 2. As a runbook fragment for runbooks that span regions or model variants. 3. For product and platform roadmap planning—use the canvas outputs to prioritize capacity, caching, and quantization work. Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net Patterns and Runbook Summary:

This page documents the Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net design pattern, associated capacity planning guidance, operational tooling integrations, and an actionable SRE runbook for managing high-consumption error budgets across multi-tenant inference services. The pattern is intended to reduce blast radius, keep critical customers online, and defer costly capacity purchases while enforcing reliability commitments.

Scope and audience:
- SREs responsible for inference-serving SLOs and multi-tenant capacity governance
- Platform/product owners defining SLO contracts for tenants
- Incident commanders and oncall engineers who execute capacity and throttling actions

Problem statement:
As inference workloads become more heterogeneous, single-threshold error-budget triggers either overreact (unnecessary capacity spend) or underreact (missed mitigations). A tiered safety-net provides graduated mitigations mapped to business impact and tenancy class.

 - Latency SLO (p95 tail for token completion): <200ms for interactive, <500ms for batch embeddings.

 - Advisory (>=30% consumed): notifications, suggested knob recommendations, additional telemetry collection.
 - Protective (>=70% consumed): soft preemption of lowest-priority requests, enable conservative batching heuristics, spin up elastic reserved nodes.
 - Emergency (>=100% consumed or sustained

PRD: Session Resilience and Fallback Contract for Transactional LLM Endpoints Summary ------- This PRD defines the Session Resilience and Fallback Contract for transactional (single-shot and short-session) LLM endpoints. The goal is to ensure predictable customer-visible behavior when the primary model or serving tier cannot meet request SLOs due to load, partial outages, or degraded model fidelities. Key objectives - Provide a deterministic, auditable fallback policy that preserves latency SLOs and minimizes cost while bounding user-visible degradation. - Define an API-level contract and response semantics for fallback events so SDKs and client integrations can programmatically observe, surface, and respond. - Specify telemetry, tracing, and QA requirements required for safe rollout. Non-goals - This PRD does not prescribe specific quantization techniques or kernel-level runtime changes; implementation may leverage existing Optimize recommendations. - Not covering long conversational session transfer semantics (that belongs to Conversation Session PRD). Unhandled model fallbacks produce inconsistent results and can break downstream workflows. - Existing fallback behavior is implicit and varies by service: sometimes requests queue, sometimes they degrade fidelity silently. This ambiguity increases support load and causes avoidable customer regressions. Overview: This playbook describes the intended behavior and operational steps for runtime-level fallback and graceful degradation across Redwood Inference deployments. It targets on-call SREs, runtime engineers, and platform product owners who must ensure applications meet latency and availability SLOs under degraded conditions (e.g., spot evictions, model OOMs, regional capacity constraints, extreme tail-latency events).
