Dependency latency attenuation playbook and operational pattern catalog Overview Purpose This playbook codifies a set of operational patterns, configuration defaults, and rollout procedures for attenuating latency volatility introduced by downstream dependencies (datastores, feature services, model shards, third-party APIs, and hardware-accelerated kernels). It is intended for service owners, SREs, and runtime engineers who own end-to-end request latency SLOs. Scope - Applies to all Redwood production services that contribute to user-facing inference latency (edge proxies, request routers, model-serving frontends, and orchestration layers). - Covers patterns for fault-tolerant latency control: time budgets, graceful degradation, hedging, caching, pipelining, rate-limiting, and backpressure. - Does NOT replace per-service runbooks; it is a catalog and prescriptive default. Scope and audience - Scope: inference-router, cost-aware-batcher, model-variant-fallback, and the traffic-shaper service. - Audience: Platform SREs, Serving Runtime, Performance Engineering, and Product engineers owning route-level SLOs. Uncoordinated burst handling either causes degraded user experience (drop/queue overflows) or large cost spikes (over-provisioning). This playbook prescribes deterministic, observable mechanisms that trade short-term admission for long-term stability. Accelerated Manager Activation Framework Summary: This document defines the Accelerated Manager Activation Framework (AMAF): a repeatable, measurable onboarding and certification path for newly promoted or newly hired people managers at Redwood Inference. AMAF is designed to reduce time-to-impact, align expectations with business goals, and provide a clear escalation and sponsor model for the first 120 days. Audience: - New managers (individual contributors promoted into manager roles or external hires with direct reports) - Their skip-levels and onboarding sponsors - People Ops and Leadership Development partners Goals and success metrics: - Achieve role-certification within 120 days for 85% of participants. - Manager ramp score (composite of direct-report feedback, 1:1 cadence adherence, and operational milestones) >= 75 by day 120. - Reduce time-to-stable-team-performance (measured by team health index) by 20% vs. legacy baseline. Overview and principles: - Sponsor-led: every new manager is paired with a senior sponsor (peer manager or director) for the first 120 days. It blends an intensive first-6-month checklist with recurring mini-feedback sprints so managers and new hires reach reliable performance, cultural alignment, and measurable outcomes faster than a standard 90-day plan. Scope and audience: - Audience: managers (IC managers, engineering managers, product managers), people-ops partners, and new hires. - Scope: first 6 months post-offer-accept through the candidate’s first performance cycle. Applies to full-time ICs, PMs, and engineering managers. Does not replace role-specific technical onboarding tracked by teams. Principles (why this exists): - Make ramp predictable: define clear signals of readiness and objective milestones. - High-frequency feedback reduces misunderstandings and accelerates behavior change. - Manager accountability: managers own the integration outcome and coordinate cross-functional onboarding. - Lightweight, repeatable rituals that scale across teams. Outcomes and success metrics (examples): - Time-to-first-merge for engineers: median target 3 weeks for small fixes, 8 weeks for core-area contributions. - First 6-month performance-readiness: 85% of hires rated “on-track” or higher in manager checkpoint. - New-hire satisfaction (pulse): Net Promoter Score (NPS) >= 30 after 90 days. This document catalogs the set of platform operator tooling that the eng-platform team endorses for accelerating operator workflows, reduces cognitive load during incidents, and improves MTTR for LLM inference services. It also gives a recommended adoption playbook, runbook snippets, dashboard templates, and measured success criteria. The goal is to standardize operator tooling across regions and reduce bespoke scripts and ad-hoc consoles.

Background and motivation:

Over 2025 we observed recurring patterns where operators spent 40–60% of incident time on low-value tasks: cross-region context gathering, tenant debit reconciliation, and manual KV-cache shard rebalancing. Several pockets of automation were introduced ad-hoc, but lack of a curated, supported catalog slowed uptake and caused duplication. This catalog is the first-team curated offering to accelerate workflows while preserving operator autonomy.

Scope:

- Included: operator-facing CLI tools, web UIs, lightweight agent helpers, dashboard templates, and runbook snippets that integrate with our runtime and telemetry.
- Excluded: customer-facing consoles, vendor-only closed-source tools that cannot be audited by engineering.

Principles for inclusion:

1. Observable: every tool must emit standardized telemetry (tool.name, tool.action, request_id) to telemetry.ingest.platform-tools.
2. Reversible: actions that modify runtime state must be reversible or provide an automated rollback within 5 minutes.
3. ACL-aware: use RBAC hooks in platform-authz; no tool bypasses tenant isolation checks.
4. Test-first: every tool must have a synthetic /test endpoint and a canary release in a staging region.

Catalog (short descriptions and recommended owners):

- op-inspect (CLI) — a single-command cross-region context aggregator. Pulls traces, last 50 requests, and cost meters for a given tenant. Owner: platform-telemetry.

Fidelity & Cost Telemetry Advisor: Launch Brief and Playbook Summary:

This brief defines the product scope, acceptance criteria, launch steps, and go-to-market signals for the Fidelity & Cost Telemetry Advisor (FCTA) — a lightweight advisor service surfaced in Console and via API that recommends fidelity (model variant, quantization, batching) and pricing/packaging guidance based on live telemetry and customer goals. The target release is a controlled launch to pilot customers with a wider availability in Q3 2026.

Background and problem statement:
- Customers struggle to tune fidelity vs. cost tradeoffs for production inference. Current approaches are manual (trial-and-error) or require deep engineering investment.
- Platform telemetry contains rich signals (latency distributions, token-per-request distributions, KV cache hit rates, warm-start ratios, error rates) that can be turned into actionable fidelity recommendations.

Goals and non-goals:
1. Goals:
 - Surface per-route fidelity recommendations that reduce per-token cost by 10–30% while keeping customer-defined quality constraints (BLEU/ROUGE/QA delta) within tolerance.
 - Provide clear, actionable rollout steps (canary traffic split, metric watchers, rollback triggers).
 - Integrate with pricing engine to estimate monthly $ savings and recommended packaging options (microbundle, warm-capacity suggestion).
2. Non-goals:
 - This release will not provide automated model-level retraining nor automated quantization of customer models.
 - The advisor will not automatically change production traffic (manual approval required).

Success metrics (KPIs):

It provides a step-by-step runbook for safely limiting tenant resource consumption while maintaining the best possible service for remaining traffic. It documents service-level thresholds, decision logic, implementation knobs, and monitoring / runbook steps. Goals - Keep latency-sensitive endpoints responsive under stress with graceful, testable quality reductions. - Make degradations predictable and auditable: every fallback path must be covered by automated tests, rollout rules, and metrics. - Optimize for user-perceived utility first, cost second: prefer semantic-preserving fallbacks over blind truncation. - Provide a single canonical implementation and configuration schema used by hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Scope Applies to: Redwood API generation endpoints (including streaming), chat APIs, dedicated model routes, and runtime-sidecar behaviors for Private deployments. Excluded: offline batch embeddings and long-running fine-tune jobs. When to invoke progressive degradation 1) System-level triggers: - Queue growth above the "elastic latency" threshold for N consecutive 10s windows (see SLOs below). - GPU preemption or node drain with remaining capacity < 30% of normal pool for more than 60s. - Downstream KV cache (>75% miss rate) causing token compute amplification. 2) Request-level triggers: - Excessive user-specified max_tokens that would materially violate latency SLO. - High cost-of-completion (estimated tokens * model-cost > per-request cap). High-level fallback sequence (ordered by preference) 1) Prefer prefix/KV cache reuse: route to cached response or partial KV warm path. 2) Model variant swap: same-architectural family, smaller parameterization or higher quantization;

shift=10%:standard 3) Reduce batch sizes for latency‑sensitive endpoints to avoid tail latency amplification (config: max_batch_tokens = 512 -> 256). 4) Schedule a cross‑functional sync (oncall + runtime + product) within 2 hours if burn persists. Phase 2 — Controlled Throttling and Customer Measures (Severe burn) 1) Activate token‑level throttles: set per‑tenant rate limit to historical 95th percentile requests/min. 2) Enable graceful fallback models (quantized or smaller model variants) for at‑risk routes via the smart routing policy. 3) Initiate customer impact triage: identify top 10 tenants by QPS and surface to CS/AE. 4) Begin incremental removal of non‑critical background workloads (e.g., refresh embeddings jobs) from the shared pool. 5) Document all changes in the incident ticket with timestamps and owners. Phase 3 — Emergency Capacity Injection and Tenant Evacuation (Emergency burn) 1) Request emergency capacity from capacity on‑call: escalate to Platform Manager with current SLO burn graph and cost/latency tradeoff. 2) If additional capacity unavailable, start tiered tenant evacuation: move non‑priority tenants to best‑effort pool or temporarily suspend heavy features per approved evacuation playbook. 3) Coordinate an external customer communication (CS drafts) for impacted enterprise customers. 4) If a production rollback is relevant (e.g., problematic rollout), follow the deployment rollback runbook and pin to prior model version. Secondary operator triggers: ongoing customer complaints, QBR-discovered regressions, or core dump events on model-worker. Defined degradation modes (ordered by impact):
1) Soft response shaping (least impact)
- Purpose: reduce per-request token work and tail latency without changing model variant.
- Actions: enforce per-request max_tokens=128, enable response-truncation plugin, set sampling temperature to 0.6 for non-core routes.
- When to use: brief latency spikes under 10m.

2) Prefix/KV cache priming and aggressive reuse
- Purpose: increase cache hit ratio to lower token compute.
- Actions: enable block-level prefix caching, increase kv-cache.eviction_threshold to 80%, extend KV TTL from 30s -> 180s for stable routes.
- Risk: stale conditional outputs for stateful sessions; only enabled for idempotent routes.

3) Model-variant fallback (preferred automated fallback)
- Purpose: route requests to a compatible, lower-cost/latency model variant (quantized or smaller topology).
- Actions: model-router updates routing table to prefer model-v1-lite then model-v1-quant if v1-full cross-SLO. Update request headers: x-rw-fallback-reason.
- Validation: check syntactic compatibility with function-calling and tool contracts.

4) Route-level shedding / throttling
- Purpose: protect core business traffic by throttling best-effort routes.
- Actions: apply per-route rate-limits, enable token-bucket fairness for tenant classes, downgrade free-tier keys to background queue.

5) Capacity eviction and autoscale failover (most disruptive)
- Purpose: reclaim GPU/CPU for critical services and activate reserved capacity.
- Actions: cordon non-critical nodes, trigger reserved GPU pool warmup, preempt batch workloads, migrate stateful model shards to hot nodes.

SLOs and Behavioral Guarantees ------------------------------ - High-priority routes (SLO tier 1): 99th-percentile tail latency <= 120ms for short-text generation (<= 256 tokens) under 95% of steady-state operating windows. - Capacity preservation: soft-quota system must reduce best-effort acceptance rate such that SLO violation rate for tier 1 remains below 0.5% during sustained bursts. - Observable fallback: every automatic degradation step must emit an event with reason, tenant_id, route_id, and before/after model variants. Standards (what must be implemented) ----------------------------------- 1) Soft-Quota Mechanics - Each tenant has two budgets: steady_budget (tokens/min) and burst_budget (tokens/min) with burst replenishment decaying over 15 minutes. - Admission probability p = min(1, steady_budget_remaining / expected_request_cost). When burst_budget exists, p += burst_boost, capped at 1.0. - Probabilistic rejection responses must return HTTP 429 with header X-Redwood-Admission: soft-quota and JSON body describing the expected retry-after and a recommended fallback (model variant id). 2) Eviction Credits and Ordering - Best-effort workloads (non-tier-1) accumulate eviction credits over time at a configurable rate (default: 1 credit / 10s of active worker time). - On pressure, runtime claims credits in LIFO order from the most-recently-scheduled best-effort slices to prioritize longer-lived allocations for reclamation. - Eviction actions prefer graceful demotion over hard kill: reduce batch sizes, cancel queued requests (with a cancel-callback to client), then drain worker slot and release MIG slice. 3) Graceful Degradation Ladder (examples) - Step 0 (transparent): opportunistic batching increase or tiny delay (<5ms) to absorb variance. - Step 1 (batch shape): request-level batch_size cap lowered to preserve latency for tail

reduce memory pressure. - batch-size-limit: cap continuous-batching window to preserve latency. - soft-throttle-embeddings: reduce embedding concurrency. - cost-airgap: suspend non-essential billing-intensive background jobs. 3) Policy primitives - trigger: metric + comparator + duration (e.g., node_gpu_util > 92% for 30s). - priority: integer ranking of degraders; lower = higher precedence. - scope: tenant | node | control-plane | region. - duration: intended degrade duration and max_auto_rollback window (e.g., 5m, 30m, 2h). - cooldown: minimum time after an auto-rollback before re-applying same policy. Service degradation and fallbacks runbook Overview: This runbook codifies how Redwood SREs detect, respond to, and recover from service degradation events while preserving user experience and protecting SLOs. It defines degradation modes, alert-to-action mappings, automated tooling, capacity and routing mitigations, and post-incident review requirements. Scope and applicability: - Applies to all public inference frontends (api.redwood.ai), model-serving clusters (serving-gpu-*, serving-cpu-*), and the routing control plane (router-svc). - Not intended for scheduled maintenance (see maintenance runbook) or non-production clusters. On-call contacts and ownership: - Primary on-call: inference-sre rotation (PagerDuty: PD#inf-sre). - Escalation: SRE Lead (Marco Liu), Platform Eng Manager (Priya Reddy). - Exec notification threshold: sustained >=5% P99 latency regression for 30+ minutes or error-rate contributing >20% monthly error budget burn. Key definitions and SLO mappings: - Availability SLO (external): 99.9% success ratio for generation endpoints, measured as (2xx responses)/(all non-4xx client errors) per 30d window. - Latency SLOs: P95 < 150ms, P99 < 600ms for short-form generation (<=256 tokens). - Error budget: monthly token-weighted budget; alerts tied to burn-rate >3x sustained for 30m. SafeMode Degrader and Fallback Orchestration Playbook SUMMARY This document describes the SafeMode Degrader (SMD) — an operator-facing and automated orchestration subsystem used in Redwood private deployments to gracefully degrade service capabilities under capacity, thermal, or upstream network stress. It defines the decision trees, policy primitives, SLO thresholds, observability signals, deployment & testing steps, and rollback guidance for on-prem and VPC installations. Use case and scope - Primary goal: keep customer-facing APIs available and predictable by trading off non-essential or expensive work (large-model variants, long-context requests, non-critical caching) when infrastructure signals indicate imminent SLO violations. - Scope: tenant-level and node-level degradation for Private (VPC/on-prem) control planes and runtime nodes. Emergency Deployment Authorization and Audit Retention Standard Overview:
This standard defines the authorization, audit logging, data residency, and evidence-retention requirements that apply to emergency (hotfix) deployments across Redwood Inference hosted, dedicated, and private environments. It provides clear, auditable workflows to safely expedite critical fixes while preserving forensic integrity, compliance evidence, and data residency guarantees.

Scope:
- Applies to all production-facing services and model-serving endpoints.
- Covers emergency change approvals, Just-In-Time (JIT) privilege activation, audit field schema, retention mapping, and handoff to incident response and compliance teams.
- Does not replace normal release gating; it is for timeboxed emergency actions only.

Definitions:
1) Emergency deployment: a code or configuration change required to mitigate an active incident or prevent imminent, severe degradation of service, security, or compliance.
2) JIT access: short-lived elevation of privileges to perform a specific emergency action.
3) Evidence bundle: packaged artifacts (audit logs, deployment diffs, approvals, provenance metadata) delivered to compliance and incident-response post-event.

Principles:
- Principle of least privilege: only the minimum set of privileges required for the emergency action are granted, and they are time-limited.
- Audit-first: every emergency action must be observable and reconstructible; logging requirements are non-negotiable.
- Residency-preserving: emergency actions must maintain data residency constraints; if an action temporarily moves data or telemetry cross-border, the action must be pre-approved by Legal/Privacy.
- Traceable approvals: all approvals must be cryptographically or digitally auditable (ticket systems + SSO identity).

Roles and responsibilities:
- Engineering oncall (service owner): initiates emergency request, performs mitigation under JIT access, captures deployment artifacts.
- Oncall authorizer (senior engineer or team lead): approves emergency JIT access and scope;

Residency and RBAC Synchronization Playbook Overview:
This playbook defines the operational model, policies, and runbook for synchronizing role-based access control (RBAC) and audit logging with data residency and retention requirements across multi-region Redwood deployments. It ties together authorization metadata, audit stream configuration, secure storage residency, and incident response evidence workflows so that access decisions, logs, and retained evidence remain correlated and auditable for regulatory and customer obligations.

Scope and applicability:
- Applies to: hosted API, Dedicated, and Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments that host customer data subject to residency or retention obligations.
- Services in-scope: authz-service, access-indexer, audit-stream, residency-controller, evidence-orchestrator, kv-audit-store.
- Exclusions: ephemeral debug logs that do not contain user identifiers (see Appendix: log classification).

Principles:
1. Single source of truth: authorization policies and residency labels are authoritative in the residency-controller; other services must synchronize from it.
2. Log locality and index continuity: audit events must be stored in a region-aligned, tamper-evident store and indexed for fast retrieval.
3. Evidence binding: compliance evidence required for audits must include the RBAC snapshot, log anchors, and a residency oath at the time of the event.

ARERP ensures exceptions are timeboxed, risk-assessed, and evidence-backed so the company maintains auditability and minimal exposure. Scope: - Temporary changes to role assignments that grant expanded privileges (RBAC exceptions) - Requests to store or process data in locations outside standard residency zones (Residency exceptions) - Deviations from documented retention schedules for specific datasets (Retention exceptions) - Any exception that affects audit logging posture or requires changes to collection/retention of logs Actors and Responsibilities: - Requester: Individual or team initiating the exception (owner must be a manager-level engineer or product lead). - Security Reviewer: Security team member who performs risk assessments and recommends controls. - Data Privacy Lead: Evaluates residency and legal/regulatory constraints. - Approver: Designated approver(s) depending on risk tier (see Decision Matrix). - System Owner: Service/account owner responsible for implementing and reverting changes. - Audit Owner: Responsible for ensuring evidence (logs, approvals) is retained. This cookbook provides concrete, copy-pasteable guidance for instrumenting Redwood SDK clients (all official language SDKs) with telemetry and observability signals that are compatible with our platform dashboards and SLOs. It focuses on three goals:

- Make failures diagnosable quickly by on-call engineers.
- Ensure cost and latency metrics are available at token/route/model granularity.
- Keep client-side telemetry low-overhead and privacy-conscious.

Audience:
- SDK authors and maintainers
- Integrations engineers and partner SDKs
- Solutions engineers helping customers instrument clients

Key signals (what we collect and why):

1) Request lifecycle events (traceable per request)
- request.start — when the SDK begins network work
- request.end — on successful completion
- request.error — on final failure
Purpose: Build traces across client -> Redwood gateway -> serving runtime for latency breakdowns and root-cause analysis.

2) Token & response metrics
- tokens.prompt, tokens.completion (counts)
- bytes_sent, bytes_received
Purpose: Chargeback, cost attribution, and anomaly detection for sudden token spikes.

3) Model variant & config metadata
- model_id, model_variant, quantization_profile, max_tokens, temperature
Purpose: Link client calls to model performance profiles and audit regressions after rollouts.

4) Sampling of interactions for quality monitoring
- hashed-session-id, prompt-hash, response-hash (not raw text)
Purpose: Allow fuzzed sampling for evals and guardrails while preserving PII constraints.

- Minimal synchronous hooks: provide blocking hooks that fire before the network call and after the response/error. Keep payloads small (IDs, counts, timings).
- Async background uploads: aggregate and upload telemetry in batches (default 30s or 250 events, whichever comes first).
- Respect user privacy: do not send raw prompt or response text unless explicitly enabled via an opt-in API and

Telemetry Golden Set and Lint Runbook for SDKs Overview: This runbook defines the Telemetry Golden Set (TGS) and the telemetry-lint gating process used by the Developer Experience (DevX) and Observability teams to keep SDK telemetry stable, high-fidelity, and actionable. The TGS is a curated, executable collection of canonical events and assertions that represent the minimum viable telemetry for each SDK release surface (auth, request, streaming, error, and cost). The lint rules verify schema, sampling, and cardinality constraints before merge and during canary. Goals: - Ensure telemetry events emitted by SDKs conform to schema and naming conventions. - Prevent regressions that cause metric loss, alert noise, or ingestion spikes. - Provide fast local and CI feedback with reproducible golden cases. - Make telemetry changes discoverable, reviewed, and backwards-compatible. Scope and ownership: - Applies to: all official Redwood SDKs (Python, Go, Node, Java). - Owned by: DevX Observability (primary), SDK Owners (secondary). - CI gates enforced in: ci/telemetry-golden-check (pre-merge), ci/telemetry-canary (post-merge). Definitions: - Telemetry Golden Set (TGS): a suite of 12–30 canonical event payloads + assertions per SDK that exercise common and edge behavior. Each payload has a unique id in the repo under /telemetry/golden/ and a human-readable description. - telemetry-lint: the validation tool used in local and CI pipelines to run schema checks, delta analysis, and sampling verification. Required signals in every SDK TGS (minimum): 1) sdk.init (startup) — includes sdk.version, platform, commit_sha. 2) request.start, request.end — includes route_id, model_name, token_count_estimate. 3) stream.chunk (if streaming) — includes sequence, bytes, is_final. 4)

Cause: client stripped headers (proxies or CORS) or client used custom HTTP client without propagation. Fix: document header requirements in integration guide and add SDK instrumentation tests that assert header presence. - Symptom: High 95th token latency. Telemetry ingestion and retention guidelines Summary

This document defines Redwood Inference’s standard for telemetry ingestion, storage tiers, retention windows, and sampling/aggregation rules across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. It is intended for platform engineers, SRE, and product owners who operate instrumented services (API gateways, runtime, routers, and model-serving agents). The goal is to make telemetry useful for debugging and SLOs while controlling storage and egress costs.

Goals

- Ensure production-grade observability with predictable cost.
- Maintain signal fidelity for SLO, incident response, and regression detection.
- Provide consistent cross-service schemas to enable multi-service correlation.
- Standardize retention, sampling, and rollouts so teams can plan for budgets and audits.

Scope

Applies to:
- Metrics (Prometheus-style time series)
- Traces (OpenTelemetry spans)
- Structured logs and events (JSON messages from services and agents)
- Model-serving telemetry (per-request tokens, model-id, quantization profile, batch id)

Not in scope: debug-only ephemeral traces from local developer runs unless uploaded intentionally.

Definitions

- Ingestion pipeline: components that accept telemetry, perform enrichment, sampling, and forward to storage backends.
- Tiered retention: hot/fast (7–30 days), warm (31–90 days), cold (90–365 days), archive (>365 days, customer opt-in).
- Cardinality: effective unique label combinations. High-cardinality labels must be gated.

Principles

1) Enforce bounded cardinality by default.
- Use synthetic IDs or hashed identifiers for high-cardinality attributes (user_id -> user_id_hash_8).
2) Optimize for SLO observability.
- Keep raw traces for error SLO windows (30 days) and aggregated metrics longer.
3) Cost-aware defaults.
- All services inherit platform defaults; teams must request exemptions with a cost justification.
4) Deterministic sampling and deterministic routing.
- Sampling decisions include a deterministic sample key to allow rehydration for specific request ids.

Coordination & Telemetry Gateway + Circuit Breaker Playbook Summary:

This playbook describes a coordinated runtime pattern we call the Coordination & Telemetry Gateway (CTG) and its paired Circuit Breaker (CB) policies. The goal is to provide a single control point for cross-cutting decisions (routing, degrade/fallback, and kernel-scheduling hints) while centralizing telemetry collection and defensive circuit-breaking for overload and kernel regressions.

Use cases:
- Protect downstream kernel pools from noisy/malicious traffic or sudden microbursts.
- Attach coherent telemetry and causal metadata to requests to enable rapid attribution during profiling and post-incident analysis.
- Provide safe, automated fallbacks (model variant, reduced tokens, synchronous->async) with audit trail.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and Dedicated deployments; CTG is optional in Private but recommended as a light control-plane sidecar.
- Integrates with existing services: rt-gateway, kernel-scheduler, kv-cache-manager, telemetry-proxy, and the runtime orchestration plane.
- Assumes request metadata (route, token_count_estimate, customer_tier, affinity_tag) is available at ingress.

High-level architecture (text diagram):

Client -> rt-gateway -> CTG (coordination + telemetry-proxy) -> kernel-scheduler -> kernels (GPU pool)
 
CTG components:
- Ingress policy evaluator (rate limits, tenant priority, canary rules)
- Telemetry enrichment & sampler (adds request provenance, flags, and sampling decisions)
- Circuit-breaker engine (per-route/per-tenant, token/latency/error triggers)
- Kernel hint emitter (sends priority, batch_hint, prefetch_hint to kernel-scheduler)
- Fallback orchestrator (model variant & routing decisions; delegates to routing table)

Design goals and constraints:
- Deterministic decision surface: given identical request metadata, CTG must make repeatable routing and CB decisions.
- Low added latency: CTG target p95 additional latency < 1.5ms for simple passes; complex policy evaluation gated behind a fast-path.
- Observability-first: every circuit or fallback decision

Runtime telemetry sampling and cost-aware profiling policy Summary ------- This document defines Redwood's standardized policy for runtime telemetry sampling and cost-aware profiling. It describes which signals to collect, how to sample requests to meet SLOs while controlling telemetry costs, recommended storage/retention tiers, and an operational runbook for changes or incidents that require higher-fidelity traces. The goal is to preserve diagnostic signal for engineering and SRE workflows while bounding observability costs and avoiding unbounded ingestion/ingress spikes. Motivation and goals -------------------- - Reduce observability spend growth while retaining high utility for performance and regression investigations. - Provide deterministic, auditable sampling behavior across runtime components (dispatcher, kernel dispatcher, kvcache, model-handler). - Make profiling decisions workload-aware: bursty clients, tail-heavy routes, canary experiments, and high-cost model variants should get more coverage. - Define safe escalation and rollback paths when increased telemetry is required during incidents or experiments. Telemetry signals (priority list) -------------------------------- 1) High-value, low-volume (always-on) - Per-request SLO metadata: request_id, route, model_variant, tenant, priority_class, latency_ms, status_code - Aggregated token-level counters: tokens_requested, tokens_emitted per model_variant (1s rollup) 2) Medium-value (sampled) - Traces for inference lifecycle across runtime components (dispatcher -> kernel -> device) - Kernel queue times and kernel execution durations (p50/p95/p99 histograms) 3) Low-value / expensive (adaptive sampling) - Full step-level GPU kernel traces (PTX/cupti-level) and per-op GPU timelines - Full request payloads and user prompt text (redaction rules apply) Sampling strategy overview -------------------------- We use a hybrid deterministic+adaptive sampling strategy: a low base sample rate plus deterministic upsampling for classes of requests that

KV cache hit ratio (operational metric): >= 85% for steady-state batch-driven workloads - Telemetry data budget: < 5 GB/day per 1000 qps baseline (default) - Alerting thresholds (examples): - Latency P95 > 300ms for > 5 minutes -> Sev2 - Error rate > 1% for > 3 minutes -> Sev2 - Telemetry egress spike > 200% of daily baseline -> Follow cost-exposure playbook Telemetry sampling policy (slim default) 1. Metrics: 100% of critical metrics (latency histograms, error counters, KV cache metrics, GPU utilization) are emitted at 10s aggregation windows. 2. Traces: Adaptive head-based sampling at 5% baseline across tenants. During canary or incident investigations the sampling rate may be increased up to 100% for affected tenant-id(s) for a bounded window (default 15 minutes) via operator command. 3. Logs: Error logs (>= WARNING) are forwarded 100%. INFO/DEBUG logs are sampled at 1% by default and retained locally for 72 hours before pruning. 4. Full prompt text capture requires explicit customer consent and a separate evidence bundle workflow. Admission Insight and Decision Telemetry for Scheduler Summary: This page documents the admission and decision-level telemetry requirements for Redwood's kernel scheduler admission controller. It defines the health signatures we rely on for proactive alerting, the canonical decision trace payloads emitted by the scheduler, guidance for downstream consumers (SRE, monitoring, and profiling pipelines), and an operational runbook for incidents that start with admission anomalies. Goals: - Make admission behavior observable, debuggable, and auditable without heavy sampling. - Provide deterministic signals for automated scaling and QoS fallbacks. - Standardize the decision payload so cross-team tooling (benchmarks, profilers, incident triage) can reason about admission outcomes. Scope: Applies to: kernel admission controller (admission-layer that decides whether a request is accepted, queued, shed, or routed to fallback), prioritization hooks, and admission-related sidecars that mediate kernel selection. Regression is not reproducible under controlled conditions OR attributable to harness variance and fixed --- ## Bisect strategy (finding the change) ### A. Flag-based bisect (fast path) 1) Force `kernel_mode=baseline` while keeping everything else constant 2) Force `kernel_mode=fp8` (or `int8`) with autoselect disabled 3) Toggle autoselect heuristics on/off 4) Toggle scheduler knobs to previous defaults (batching window/backpressure) Interpretation: - Regression persists in baseline → likely scheduler or infra - Regression appears only in fp8/int8 forced mode → kernel path / quant profile - Regression appears only with autoselect enabled → heuristic bug (wrong regime mapping) ### B. SLO-driven runtime contracts and rollback playbook Summary This document defines a practice for tying public service/API contract changes to SLO-driven runtime acceptance gates and an operational rollback playbook. It standardizes how we declare the runtime impact of API/model/runtime changes, what telemetry must be collected, automated gate thresholds, and the exact steps engineers must follow to roll back or mitigate when gates fail. Scope - Applies to changes that alter runtime behavior or the request/response contract for Redwood-hosted inference endpoints and to configuration changes in Dedicated and Private runtime sidecars. - Includes: new streaming semantics, structured response version bumps, batch/quantization profile switches, kernel scheduling changes, fallback routing, and autoscaling policy changes. - Excludes purely UI-only changes and documentation-only edits. Motivation Making rollout decisions based on signal close to the customer experience reduces blast radius. Historically we relied on ad-hoc dashboards and team conventions; this playbook enforces: - a single source of truth for contract impact metadata declared during PRs; - automated SLO gates enforced in CI/CD and at canary runtime; - a repeatable, fast rollback path with clear ownership. Definitions - Contract change class (CC): small | compatible | incompatible | runtime-affecting. Each change must be labeled in the PR. - Runtime acceptance gate: an automated check that evaluates production-canary telemetry against SLOs for a change window. - Canary window: default 15 minutes for high-risk changes, 60 minutes for low-risk changes (configurable per change). - Primary SLOs: availability (p99 success rate), latency (p99), error budget burn. Forensic Escalation and Capacity Hedging Playbook Summary:

This playbook defines a combined forensic-escalation and capacity-hedging procedure for production incidents that threaten SLOs for inference services (hosted, dedicated, and private deployments). It codifies: escalation responsibilities, evidence collection standards for post-incident review, automated and manual capacity hedging actions, and an error-budget-aware decision matrix for graceful degradation. This doc is intended for SREs on-call, on-call leads, runtime engineers, and incident commanders.

Scope and applicability:

- Services in scope: inference-router, batch-scheduler, kv-cache-service, model-runtime-pool, burst-absorber, traffic-router.
- Environments: prod (all regions), pre-prod only when configured with production traffic mirroring.
- This playbook applies when any of the following SLOs are at risk: 99th-percentile latency, p95 latency > SLO, availability (5xx rate), or sustained error-budget burn.

Quick reference (TL;DR):

1) If an alert indicates SLO degradation and burn rate > 3x sustained for 10m, declare a Sev-2 and execute hedging steps A–C.
2) If burn rate > 5x in a 30m window or p99 latency > 3x SLO, declare Sev-1 and escalate to oncall lead + infra lead; begin emergency capacity hedging and traffic reroute.
3) Collect forensic evidence in parallel (traces, key metrics, GPU utilization, server-side logs, KV hit-rate snapshots).

Escalation matrix and ownership:

- First responder (on-call SRE): initial triage, apply pre-authorized hedging actions, collect evidence.
- On-call lead: decision to elevate to Sev-1, coordinate cross-team owners, approve cost-impacting hedges.
- Runtime infra owner: responsible for executing pool scale-ups, patch rollbacks, and kernel toggles.
- Product impact lead: assesses functional degradation risk and communicates to customer-success as needed.

Service-Anchored Onboarding Eval Contract with Regression Contingency Overview ======== This document defines a service-anchored evaluation contract used during model onboarding and promotion for production serving. It couples acceptance criteria (quality, latency, token-cost) with an explicit regression contingency playbook so that any release can be validated and, if necessary, automatically mitigated or rolled back with low human overhead. The goal is to make onboarding decisions auditable, repeatable, and safe across Hosted, Dedicated and Private deployment modes. Why a service-anchored contract? - Aligns model promotion to concrete product-facing SLOs rather than abstract metric thresholds. - Ensures cross-functional sign-off (SRE, Product, Applied ML, Platform) with traceable artifacts. - Ties continuous evals, shadow traffic, and canary sampling to an actionable regression escalation path. Scope ----- Applies to: - New model variants promoted to staging/canary for inference (hosted/dedicated/private). - Quantized artifacts and hybrid-precision builds. - Functional changes to prompt templates or response post-processing that affect user-visible outputs. Exclusions: - Research-only checkpoints not intended for production. - Infrastructure-only kernel upgrades that do not change model weights or prompt behavior (see infra change process). Core concepts and definitions ---------------------------- - Service owner: owner of the product endpoint (e.g., search-relevance, chat-assistant). - Eval contract: a checklist and thresholds mapping to service SLOs used to accept or reject a promotion. - Shadow validation: live traffic duplicated to the candidate model with telemetry capture only (no user-facing outputs). - Regression: any statistically significant negative delta in an agreed-upon slice of metrics that crosses the impact budget. Eval contract template (summary)

Retention: snapshot of 72 hours around incident saved to incident artifacts storage. --- Post-incident process & QBR inclusion 1) Immediate post-incident (within 24 hours): - Incident timeline and responsible owners posted to ticket. - Customer-facing summary drafted by CSM and approved by engineering for accuracy. - Short-term mitigations documented and follow-up tickets created for permanent fixes. 2) Root cause analysis (within 5 business days): - Full timeline, contributing factors, and a 3-point corrective action plan (short, medium, long term). - Identify whether regression was caused by model change, infra, config, or customer behavior. - Assign owners and target dates for remediation. 3) QBR / Health Check inclusion (next scheduled QBR): - Include incident summary, customer impact metrics, remediation status, and CSAT follow-up. - Present changes to SLOs or operational controls if required (e.g., new routing policies, additional observability). 4) Severity reclassification and SLA reconciliation: - Confirm final severity (may be downgraded after RCA). - Reconcile any SLA credits or contractual

Postmortem owner: writes final RCA and follow-ups. Immediate runbook checklist (pattern-based) Use this checklist when the alert matches a known pattern. If not, shift to regression triage flow. - Verify monitoring (Grafana /datadog) is accurate. - Capture a p99/p95/p50 snapshot and recent deployment IDs. - Check model-serving nodes: `rmi list --service redwood-runtime | grep unhealthy` - If CPU/GPU saturation: trigger scale policy `infra autoscale --service runtime --up 2` - If errors spike and correlate with new deploy: roll back to last stable tag `kubectl set image ...` Regression triage checklist (unknown pattern) 1. Collect evidence: traces, example requests, logs. Use `logs query --svc <svc> --last 30m --filter error`. 2. Identify change vectors: deploys, config changes, infra events, third-party failures. 3. Reproduce locally with traffic replay (if safe) or synthetic requests. 4. If reproducible: implement temporary routing or throttling as containment. 5. Record hypothesis and test results in the timeline. Postmortem template (lightweight) - Title: [Service] outage YYYY-MM-DD - Severity: P1/P2 - Summary (one para): what happened, customer impact, duration - Timeline (bullet list): ordered actions with timestamps and owners - Root cause hypothesis: short statement - Evidence: logs, traces, graphs (links) - Corrective actions (5 items max): owner + ETA - Preventative work: larger initiatives for backlog - Lessons learned (3 bullets): what to change in runbook/alerts/rotations Postmortem quality bar - Draft within 72 hours, owner assigned. - Include at least one reproducible signal and a concrete test to prevent regression. - Scorecard (0–5): completeness, evidence, actionability, timeline clarity, follow-up

SEV2 escalation to runtime team - eviction_queue_length > 1000 for 5m -> SEV2 to infra and runtime - sudden increase in cost per token > 50% vs baseline for 1h -> billing & product notify Canary and rollout guidance When changing fallback policies or adding new fallback variants, follow this phased rollout: 1. Internal canary: 0.5% of traffic routed to canary policy within non-customer-facing sandbox tenants for 24–48h. 2. Beta tenants: select 2–3 low-risk customers (with agreed rollback) for 48–72h. 3. Gradual ramp: 5% -> 25% -> 50% -> 100% over a minimum of 7 days, with automated abort on metric regressions. Automated abort criteria (example): - fallback_rate increases > 2x baseline and absolute > 1% for 10m. - p99 latency regresses > 20% and absolute > SLO for 15m. - end-to-end user error rate increases > 0.5% absolute for 30m. This cookbook documents Redwood Inference's standard policy and prescriptive remediation workflows for production latency degradation incidents. - Covers tiered latency SLOs (interactive, high-throughput, background) and includes automated mitigations, manual runbook steps, rollback patterns, communication templates, and post-incident actions.

Motivation:
- Latency degradations are the most common customer-facing reliability issue for inference workloads. They can be caused by traffic spikes, model regressions, kernel hotpaths, KV cache eviction storms, or hardware/network flakiness. This cookbook standardizes a fast, low-risk response pattern.

- Emergency: burn >= 70% — aggressive actions (evict heavy tenants, fall back to cheaper model variants, apply global rate limit).

Automated Onboarding SLO Escalation & Orchestration Playbook Purpose and scope:

This playbook defines the automated orchestration and escalation process used during enterprise onboarding to ensure SLO-driven stability, fast triage, and consistent customer communication. It applies to Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments during the first 90 calendar days after provisioning, with integrations into Alerting, Pager, Ticketing, and Customer Success systems.

Key objectives:
- Detect onboarding-impacting SLO regressions automatically and reduce MTTI (mean time to identify) to under 5 minutes where possible.
- Route incidents to the right team and automation step based on severity and customer tier.
- Ensure customers see timely, transparent updates and have an engineered remediation path.
- Capture telemetry and post-incident signals into onboarding QBRs.

Definitions and SLOs monitored during onboarding:
- Availability (API success rate): target >= 99.8% per customer per 1h window; warning at 99.5%, critical at 99.0%.
- Latency (p95 generation): target <= 350ms; warning at >450ms, critical at >800ms for three consecutive minutes.
- Token error rate: target < 0.2% per model route per 1h; warning at 0.5%, critical at 1.0%.
- Model quality regressions: automated eval failure rate > 5% vs baseline on onboarding prompt set (see "Onboarding Eval Sets" reference).

Alerting and severity mapping (automated rules):
1) SEV-WARN (automated): signaled when a single SLO crosses warning threshold for a rolling 15-minute window OR a single customer sees >2x baseline error rate for 5 minutes.
 - Action: create ticket (CSIN- auto), post to #cs-monitoring channel, run quick mitigation automation (see Automation actions).
2) SEV-1 (automated human escalation): triggered when threshold crosses critical for 3 consecutive minutes

It combines atomic state checkpointing, staged model activation, transactional KMS-friendly key rotation, and automated verification gates. Scope and audience: - Scope: Tenant-facing runtime components in private deployments (inference runtime, KV cache, model store, control-plane agents, local telemetry collectors). Not in scope: physical firmware upgrades for HW (see onprem-packaging docs). - Audience: Field operators, SREs, deployment engineers, and delivery leads executing upgrades in customer environments. Prerequisites and assumptions: - Operator access to customer control plane and operator-run SSH bastion or management VPN. - Backups of model artifacts and KV state accessible in immutable object store (S3 compatible). - Snapshot tooling version >= 3.4.1 installed on operator workstation. - KMS integration supports offline wrapping/unwrapping and key-versions (see KMS rotation appendix). - Pre-approved maintenance window in calendar and customer acceptance of canary flow. High-level strategy (phases): 1) Validate and baseline: collect telemetry and pre-upgrade evidence. 2) Cold checkpoints: produce consistent, point-in-time snapshots of tenant runtime state. 3) Canary upgrade: upgrade control plane + 1–3 tenants with staged runtime activation and smoke tests. 4) Gradual roll: expand tenant upgrades in bounded waves with automated validation gates. 5) Switch-over: final atomic activation for remaining tenants with KV rehydrate and verification. 6) Fortify and evidence: preserve upgrade artifacts and run post-upgrade acceptance tests. Private Deploy Commissioning and Safety Gate Playbook Overview:

This playbook describes the commissioning and safety-gate process for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It consolidates the preflight conformance checks, packaging/attestation requirements, day-2 validation, upgrade & rollback decision criteria, and customer sign-off gates into a single operator-facing guide. Use this document to run acceptance dry-runs, provide deterministic go/no-go signals for rollouts, and capture evidence bundles for compliance reviews.

Scope:
- Applies to new private deployments (VPC and air-gapped on-prem).
- Covers: pre-install validation, initial commissioning, nightly/first-week day-2 checks, controlled upgrade decision gates, rollback triggers, and evidence collection for customers/regulators.
- Excludes tenant-level application testing (customer responsibility), but includes tenant-impacting safety checks.

Owner and contact:
- Playbook owner: eng-private-deployments (operator lead: Arjun Patel).
- Primary oncall (field ops): rotation in PagerDuty schedule "private-field-ops".
- Escalation: SRE pager -> Platform eng -> Product security.

Quick summary of safety gates (high-level):
1) Preflight PASS required: hardware attestation, network topology, and KMS handshake.
2) Install PASS required: control-plane services green, model runtime health >= 99.5% in synthetic workload.
3) Day-2 PASS required before enabling tenant burst: KV-consistency checks, prefix-cache integrity, and SLO smoke tests.

### 1. Preflight Telemetry Checks
* **Telemetry Integrity:** Verification that there are no missing mandatory telemetry keys in the last 24 hours prior to the upgrade [4].
* **Baseline Telemetry Collection:** Delivery packets for upgrades affecting model execution must include 7 days of pre-upgrade baseline metrics and traces [1].

### 2. Observability & Telemetry Ingestion Gates
* **Telemetry Completeness:** Verification that key metrics, request traces, and audit logs are present and properly attributed to the customer ID and model route [2].
* **Ingestion Latency & Health:**
  * Telemetry pipeline ingestion must occur within 60 seconds [3].
  * 99th percentile metric latency must be under 120 seconds [3] (a `telemetry.ingest.lag` > 120s triggers an investigation) [4].
* **Alert & Metric Verification:** Ingestion of metrics must be confirmed and alert sanity checks must be verified [3], establishing baseline SLO measurements and alert thresholds for the first 72 hours [2].

### 3. Canary & SLO Verification
* **Canary Telemetry Comparison:** During canary rollout, key telemetry metrics—such as p95 latency, error rates, and KV cache hit ratio—are monitored and compared to baseline values using rolling 10-minute windows [4]. (Monitoring also tracks tail token generation time and output-quality hash diffs [7].)
* **Automatic Rollback / Abort Triggers:** 
  * p95 latency increase > 20% [4].
  * Error rate increase > 0.3% sustained for 5 minutes [4] (or error rate increase > 2x baseline for 10 minutes) [7].
  * Output-quality regression or error types matching model-compatibility signatures [4, 7].

### 4. Post-Upgrade Evidence and Compliance
* **Post-Upgrade Artifact Bundle:** A bundle of telemetry artifacts covering the first 24 hours post-upgrade must be delivered [1].
* **SLO Verification Signoff:** An acceptance signoff must be completed with SLO verification marked pass/fail with measured values [1].
* **Rollback Artifact Preservation:** If an upgrade fails or triggers a rollback, telemetry artifacts from the failed upgrade window must be preserved and marked immutable for investigation, followed by a telemetry smoke test to confirm baselines are restored [1, 4].
* **PII Filtering:** Telemetry exports must be filtered for tenant PII unless full payload capture is explicitly requested by the customer with documented legal approval [1].

Focuses on observability signals, probe generation, synthetic backfill policy, and a triage runbook for applied ML teams. We observe intermittent 95th+ percentile latency spikes (tail events) that are costly and can correlate with quality regressions after quant or routing changes. Typical failure modes include KV-cache thrash, quantized kernel stalls, and rarely seeded memory pressure on GPU nodes. Root cause analysis is slow when spikes are ephemeral and requests are not reproducible. This playbook defines a reproducible capture -> probe synthesis -> synthetic backfill workflow so model-onboarding, quantization, and runtime teams can reproduce, validate, and fix tail regressions without impacting live traffic. Applies to text generation and chat endpoints served by eval-mesh and production-serving. Not in scope: unrelated network-level outages, control-plane-only incidents. Invariants: all captures must be sampled and redacted to PII policy; probes must be deterministic given seed and tokenizer version; backfill workloads must not exceed 20% of eval-fleet capacity and must be scheduled during maintenance windows unless explicitly approved. 1) Latency-tail trigger: p99 > 1.2x baseline_p99 for 5 consecutive 1-min windows OR single-request latency > 3s for short-context endpoints. 2) Quality signal: embedding cosine drift > 0.07 on monitored slices OR token-entropy change > 0.25. 3) KV-cache miss storm: cache_miss_rate increase > 10ppt for request shard. 4) Quantization suspect: runtime quant-decoded-error > 0.5% on probe samples. Steps: 1) Detection:

compatible snapshots: use snapshot-query tool `snapshot-query --tags incident:<id> --window 72h` 3) Create backfill batch: `backfill-orchestrator create --probes probes/<id>.json --window <start>:<end> --fleet-tag eval-backfill --max-concurrency 50` 4) Throttle policy: default QPS cap at 0.2x production and backfill concurrency <= 15 per model. 5) Data retention: backfill traces stored for 90 days in backfill-archive. 6) Output artifacts: per-probe response timelines, per-token latencies, kernel-time breakdown CSVs, and per-slice quality metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/Embedding drift). oncall-lagging-telemetry-reconstitution-and-synthetic-backfill-guide-2025 Overview This runbook documents the recommended approach for reconstituting lagging or missing telemetry (metrics, traces, logs, and derived tokenized telemetry) during incidents and for routine backfills. It covers safe reconstruction from persisted sources, heuristic reconstruction where direct data is missing, and running controlled synthetic backfill jobs to recreate observability coverage for short windows. The goal is to enable oncall and operators to restore signal quickly for incident triage and postmortem analysis without causing production side-effects or cost blowouts. Scope - Applies to: platform operator teams, oncall SREs, and observability engineers. - Data sources: Prometheus/Thanos metrics, Datadog traces, BigQuery/ClickHouse logs, S3/Kafka raw request logs, runtime prefix/KV cache telemetry, and tokenized-cost traces emitted by runtime. - Out of scope: reconstructing user PII; any re-ingestion that could duplicate customer billing events requires approval from finance and security. When to follow this guide 1. Dashboard shows blank/flat lines for critical SLO SLIs over a recent window (<= 6 hours). 2. Trace sampling drops to zero while upstream services responded. 3. Logging pipeline lag exceeds retention window (e.g., days) and SREs need reconstructed signal for RCA. 4. Aftermarket synthetic experiments when validating new telemetry plumbing. Quick decision matrix - If raw logs are available in S3/Kafka for the window: prefer direct reconstruction by re-parsing and reindexing into the observability store (low-risk). - If only partial metrics exist (e.g., aggregator backlog): perform heuristic reconstitution (stitch series with upstream/downstream proxies). - If critical SLIs are still missing after reconstruction: run synthetic backfill (controlled rate, dry-run first).

Latency slice synthesis and shadow benchmark specification Overview This document specifies the Latency Slice Synthesis (LSS) methodology and the Shadow Benchmark specification used by the benchmarking fleet to detect regression signals across model variants, kernel builds and scheduling policies. LSS is designed to produce reproducible latency cohorts ("slices") representative of production tail behavior while shadowing live traffic in a safe, low-impact manner. Goals - Produce stable, repeatable latency cohorts that expose kernel and scheduler regressions. - Provide a shadowing protocol that preserves customer privacy and complies with traffic quotas. - Define experiment automation, success criteria, and analysis artifacts for SRE/Runtime teams. Scope This spec applies to: hosted and dedicated runtime pools, synthetic replay harnesses, and the benchmarking fleet used during release gating. It intentionally excludes on-prem air-gapped installs (see onprem-packaging runbook). Key definitions - Latency slice: a cohort of requests grouped by features (sequence length, prompt entropy, model family, multi-turn vs single-turn) used to characterize latency distributions. - Shadow channel: a replicated execution path that runs concurrently with production but does not affect customer billing or responses. - Fidelity downgrade: intentional model/kernel setting reduction (quantization, reduced KV prefetch) used to measure graceful degradation behavior. Design principles 1) Isolation of causes: create slices that isolate sequence-length, KV-cache hit rate, and attention-kernel sensitivity. 2) Cost-aware fidelity: shadowing should consume <= 10% of a node's spare capacity and be throttled by the admission controller. 3) Observability parity: traces, kernel telemetry, and scheduler decision logs must be captured with identical tagging as production. 4)

Causal Latency Attribution and Signal Enrichment Playbook Summary and purpose This playbook defines a repeatable approach for attributing causal sources of request latency in the serving runtime and enriching traces and metrics with synthesized signals that improve root-cause diagnosis. The intended audience is runtime engineers, SREs, and profiling/product teams who investigate tail-latency incidents or validate scheduler/kernel changes against real traffic. Goals - Produce an actionable causal hypothesis for >80% of investigated tail-latency incidents within 48 hours. - Ensure enriched telemetry is available for post-incident analysis and automated detection rules within 6 hours of rollout. - Keep incremental instrumentation cost increase under 12% of telemetry budget for a standard region. Scope and non-goals - Scope: production serving runtime (request surface -> kernel dispatch -> GPU execution -> response), associated request routing, KV cache behavior, and kernel scheduling decisions. Includes streaming, chat, and embedding request shapes. - Non-goals: model-family quality regressions, client-side application logic, and offline evaluation harnesses. Quality regressions should be investigated using the eval-harness docs. Signal catalogue (what to collect) Collect the following signals for each traced request. Where possible, attach a single trace_id and request_id to correlate logs, metrics, and kernel traces. Primary signals (always-on): - request_id, trace_id, timestamp_start, timestamp_end - request_shape: token_count, prompt_length, max_decode_length, batch_size, priority_class - rpc_spans: inbound_http, auth, router, proxy-layer, runtime_api - kernel_spans: kernel_start_ns, kernel_queue_ns, kernel_execution_ns, kernel_end_ns, kernel_name - kvcache_hits: prefix_hits, kvcache_warmup_ms - gpu_counters: sm_util_pct, mem_alloc_bytes, warp_stall_cycles - host_metrics: numa_node, cpu_steal_ms, irq_drop_counts Enrichment signals (high-cardinality; sample and attach heuristics): - model_variant_hash, quantization_profile_tag, compiled_kernel_version - scheduling_decision: preempted_by,

RFSS is intended for engineering teams working on kernel scheduling, shard placement, eviction, and KV-cache warmup logic. Motivation ---------- We frequently observe complex multitenant failures and regressions that are hard to reproduce in a lab because: - Production request mixes, ordering, and interleaving matter (prefix caching, KV hits). - Heterogeneous GPU topology and eviction interactions vary by tenant co-location. - Timing-sensitive scheduler decisions (preemption, handoff) only manifest at specific concurrency shapes. RFSS gives a small, portable way to: 1) Capture a faithful snapshot of request traces + environment signals (compact capture format). 2) Re-run the captured workload in a simulator that models kernel queueing, KV-cache state, and tenant credit accounting. 3) Produce deterministic diagnostics (latency decomposition, kernel timeline, eviction traces) to accelerate triage and root cause analysis. entropy-aware-tail-sampling-and-replay-playbook Summary ------- This playbook describes an entropy-aware sampling and replay pipeline used to capture and investigate rare, high-cost tail latency events in the serving runtime. The goal is to produce a small, high-value corpus of end-to-end requests (input+context+response+runtime-trace) for offline replay, debugging, and kernel-level root-cause analysis without overwhelming storage or incurring excessive cost. Motivation ---------- Traditional frequency-based samplers either oversample common fast requests or miss low-frequency pathological requests that drive p99–p999 latency. Entropy-aware sampling combines statistical rarity in the request surface (input entropy), deviation from expected latency signatures (residual latency), and scheduler/kernel signals (unexpected kernel hops, cache misses) to prioritize traces for capture. When to use ----------- - Investigating unexplained p99+ spikes. - Prioritizing data for quantization/regression testing when corpus budget is limited. - Building reproducer sets for kernel or NVLink anomalies. Definitions and signals considered -------------------------------- - request_entropy: Shannon estimate on token distribution or prompt template fingerprint. - residual_latency: observed_latency - expected_latency(model, seq_len, tenant_profile). - kernel_hop_count: times request switched GPU kernels or was preempted. - kv_cache_miss_rate: fraction of KV lookups that missed warm caches. - cross_tenant_noise_index: normalized measure of concurrent slot contention. Sampling algorithm (high level) ------------------------------- 1. For each request, compute a sampling_score = w1 * normalized(request_entropy) + w2 * normalized(residual_latency) + w3 * normalized(kernel_hop_count) + w4 * normalized(kv_cache_miss_rate). 2. Apply a minimum threshold T_min and a dynamic reservoir budget per epoch (1h window). 3. Apply adaptive decay so that repeated requests from the same request_fingerprint are downweighted within the same epoch to protect diversity. 4. Enrich

Latency Metric Synthesis and Normalization Guide Purpose
-------
This guide standardizes how we synthesize, normalize, and interpret latency signals across the serving stack so that dashboards, alerts, and post-incident analyses compare like-for-like. It documents the telemetry fields we require, the normalization math we use for cross-model and cross-hardware comparisons, and a step-by-step triage procedure for metric anomalies.

Scope
-----
- Applies to all runtime telemetry emitted by Redwood-serving components: dispatcher, scheduler, kernel dispatcher, KV cache, model-host pools, and the network fabric observed in the control plane.
- Target audiences: runtime SREs, profiling engineers, performance QA, and anyone authoring SLOs or dashboards.

Background and motivation
-------------------------
We observed repeated confusion when correlating percentiles across heterogeneous cohorts (different model sizes, sequence lengths, and GPU classes). Raw p95/p99 numbers are insufficient because:

- different workloads have different token distributions and tail behavior;
- kernels exhibit different steady-state vs warmup profiles;
- hardware differences (A100 vs H100 vs CPU) change latency skew and variance;
- sampling biases (e.g., production sampling favoring low-entropy requests) distort percentiles.

This document prescribes: a canonical telemetry contract, normalization transforms, recommended histogram bucketing, and an investigation checklist.

Key terms and definitions
-------------------------
- SLO unit: the atomic unit we measure against (e.g., per-token generation latency for hosted-api model X at seq_len=256).
- Cohort: grouping by {model, model_variant, region, accel_class, seq_len_bucket, customer_tier}.
- Normalized latency (L_norm): latency after applying transforms to remove known covariates used for cross-cohort comparison.

-------------------------
All runtime spans/events used for latency synthesis must include the following attributes (table):

| request_id | string | unique per request | keep 30d

end-to-end-latency-attribution-using-shadow-channels-2024 Summary This playbook describes our "shadow channel" methodology for attributing end-to-end latency to internal components (kernel dispatch, NVLink latency, KV-cache misses, prefix-serialization, enqueue/dequeue overhead) without impacting production SLOs. It documents design, instrumentation, sampling, cost constraints, and an on-call runbook for triage. Scope - Applies to all hosted and dedicated model-serving clusters running the Redwood runtime. - Focus: high-p99 tail and intermittent spikes that are not explained by request size or known deployments. - Out of scope: offline microbenchmarks, model-level correctness regressions. Why shadow channels? Traditional profiling (heavy tracing on live requests) risks increased latency and cost. Shadow channels replicate a small fraction of live requests and route them through alternative, instrumented execution paths that capture per-stage timestamps and kernel-level markers, while ensuring no user-facing effects. Shadow runs are asynchronous and do not block the original request flow. Design overview 1) Sampling and routing - Global sample rate: default 0.5% of eligible requests. Adjustable per-tenant via token metadata. - Eligibility: production requests with sequence_length >= 8 and not marked internal_test or contain PII flags. - Routing: the live request continues on the low-latency path; the shadow copy is forked and sent to an instrumented runtime instance pool (shadow pool) with lower priority scheduling and strict CPU/GPU time quotas. 2) Shadow pool characteristics - Separate node label: node-role=shadow-instrumented. - Scheduler policy: preemptible, batch slicing disabled, per-request kernel trace hooks enabled. - Capacity: sized to handle worst-case sample burst for 30s at configured sample rate. Autoscaling disabled; use fixed pools to minimize

Alert thresholds and triage heuristics: - If replay kernel timeline matches production within 5% but latency differs > 15% -> investigate host-level interference (noisy neighbor) and network jitter. - If kernel variance differs > 20% -> likely scheduling non-determinism or different concurrency mix in production. Check batch-size distribution over 1 hour window. - If KV cache miss delta explains > 30% of token processing time -> treat as cache warmup issue and consider extending cache TTL for route. Re-run replay on node with isolated CPU/GPU (pinning) to rule out host noise. 3. Toggle kernel scheduling knobs: kernel_credit_limit, preemption_window_ms, eager_batching_enable. This page documents the Workload Rehearsal and Deterministic Replay Framework (WRDR). WRDR provides a safe, repeatable way to replay historical production traffic—or synthesized equivalents—against staging or canary environments to validate changes to batching, kernel selection, routing policies, and cache/quantization profiles. Why this exists:

- Unit tests and microbenchmarks miss emergent behavior from real multi-tenant traffic and inter-service dependencies.
- WRDR lets platform and runtime engineers validate regressions before large-scale rollouts and provides a forensics tool for incident reconstruction.

2) Normalization: A replay manifest normalizes variable fields (timestamps, ephemeral IDs) and optionally synthesizes client-hint variations for edge-case coverage.

The goal is to capture representative traces across latency bands and microburst events with bounded cost, enable high-fidelity replays for kernel-sensitivity debugging, and produce actionable signals for autotune and regression detection. This is operational guidance for engineers on the runtime, telemetry, and replay tooling. Why this exists - Static uniform sampling misses rare high-latency clusters and transient microbursts that correlate strongly with kernel regressions. - SLS guarantees coverage across p50/p95/p99 bands while keeping the sampling budget predictable. - Microburst sampling captures short-lived queuing spikes and NVLink/PCIe anomalies that are often the root cause of degraded tail latency. Multi‑Tenant Replay Oracle and Scheduler Debug Playbook Overview This playbook describes a deterministic replay and investigation workflow (the "Replay Oracle") for diagnosing multi‑tenant scheduler and kernel interactions that cause SLO violations or throughput regressions. It unifies capture, deterministic reconstruction, scheduler decision replay, and hypothesis-driven kernel perturbation to root cause hard‑to‑reproduce latency and fidelity issues. Audience - Oncall SREs and runtime engineers performing post‑incident forensics. - Runtime scheduler and kernel maintainers executing regressions or perf experiments. - Applied ML/evals engineers validating quality regressions caused by scheduling/economic changes. Scope and when to use this playbook Use the Replay Oracle when any of the following are true: 1) Tail latency spikes (> p99.9) recur without a clear origin in ingress or model change. 2) Multi‑tenant interference suspected (queueing patterns match but treatment varies by cohort). 3) Kernel or preemption regressions are suspected and local instrumentation is insufficient to reproduce. Signal model (what we capture) We capture a minimal, reconstructable set of signals that allow deterministic replay across layers: - Ingress event envelope: request id, route, client token, timestamp, raw prompt hash. - Scheduler trace: policy decisions, priority, admission slot id, kernel assignment hint, preemption markers. - Kernel execution trace: kernel id, launch parameters, input lengths, occupancy estimate, GPU memory deltas. - KV cache delta log: keys read/written, cache hit/miss per request. - System telemetry: GPU utilization, NVLink errors, host NIC drops, and node thermal events. Capture format and storage contract - Capture format: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) with one top-level envelope per request. Schema

Simulator components and models ------------------------------- 1) KernelQueue - Model: token-based service time model: service_time_ms = kernel_base_ms + per_token_ms * seq_len * kernel_multiplier(model_family). - Admission: takes scheduler priority and kernel credits into account. If credits insufficient, sim emits "deferred" event and queues. 2) KVCacheModel - Tracks warm/cold key sets per shard. Cache hit reduces per_token_ms by a hit_reduction_factor. Eviction follows LRU with configurable bucket sizes. 3) ShardTopology - Abstracts the mapping of requests to physical shards and NUMA domains. Topology file is loaded from the capture header and supports simulating NUMA-induced transfer penalties. 4) AdmissionController / Scheduler - Implements the same priority/credit semantics as production: token-bucket crediting, preemption thresholds, and cooperative yielding. The simulator exposes knobs: preemption_grace_ms, max_inflight_per_tenant, kernel_credit_decay_window_ms. LPFR is intended for multi-tier evaluations that exercise quantized variants, function-call behavior, long-context scenarios, and streaming/functioncall edge cases. Goals and non-goals - Goals: - Provide a telemetry contract between probe producers, federated evaluators, and the reconciliation engine so latency-sensitive probes are prioritized without starving quality coverage. - Define deterministic reconciliation rules that map probe signal patterns to automated rollback, partial isolation, or investigator escalations. - Enable mixed-precision and quant-shadow probing with cost-aware throttling and latency hedges. - Non-goals: - This is not a replacement for long-running human annotation pipelines or adjudicated safety reviews. - LPFR does not define new annotation schemas; it assumes existing probe labels and slice taxonomy. Predictive Warmstart and Cache-Hinting Architecture for Low-Latency Serving This document defines the Predictive Warmstart and Cache-Hinting architecture (PWC Architecture) designed to reduce observable tail latency and cold-start variability for multi-tenant model serving. The design couples an inference-side predictive planner with the KV-cache prefetcher and the runtime's kernel scheduler to proactively populate hot state and shape scheduling hints based on traffic predictions. Goals: - Reduce 95th and 99th percentile request latency for cold or low-traffic model variants by pre-populating KV caches and tensor allocator state before request arrival. - Provide a low-risk canary and rollout path that can be throttled per-customer or per-model. - Expose telemetry for cost vs latency trade-offs and enable automated tuning. Non-goals: - This design does not replace hardware-level warmup that requires model weight preloading. It focuses on runtime-level warmstart (KV cache, allocator priming, kernel hints) and workload-level caching policies. Applies to: hosted and dedicated runtime pools where multi-tenant scheduling and KV-cache are active. Out of scope: on-prem private deployments with strict air-gapped constraints unless customer opts in; deep model weight transformer warmups that require offline preparation. Operational observations (2024-Q4 to 2025-Q2) showed that mixed workloads with bursty conversational sessions produce repeated cold-like tails: small sessions that skip cache priming cause disproportionate tail-latency spikes and GPU kernel mispredictions. Existing approaches (heuristic ttl-based caching, on-request prefetch) either over-provision memory or introduce request-time overhead. Predictive warmstart aims to move the decision upstream to a planner that learns short-term traffic patterns and coordinates safe prefetches. High level components: - Predictive

### Conditions that Trigger Latency-Tail Capture

Latency-tail capture is initiated when any of the following conditions or signals are met [1]:

* **Latency-tail trigger:** 
  * The 99th percentile latency exceeds 1.2× the baseline p99 ($p99 > 1.2\times \text{baseline\_p99}$) for 5 consecutive 1-minute windows [1].
  * A single-request latency exceeds 3 seconds (3000 ms) for short-context endpoints [1].
* **Quality signal:** 
  * Embedding cosine drift $> 0.07$ on monitored slices [1].
  * Token-entropy change $> 0.25$ [1].
* **KV-cache miss storm:** 
  * `cache_miss_rate` increases by more than 10 percentage points (ppt) for a request shard [1].
* **Quantization suspect:** 
  * Runtime quant-decoded-error $> 0.5\%$ on probe samples [1].

---

### Limits on Synthetic Backfill

When running synthetic backfill workloads, the following limits and policies apply:

* **Capacity and scheduling:** Backfill workloads must not exceed 20% of eval-fleet capacity and must be scheduled during maintenance windows unless explicitly approved [1].
* **Historical window:** Can cover up to 72 hours of traffic centered on the first observed tail spike [1].
* **QPS cap:** Default rate limit cap is 0.2× production QPS (with an acceptable range of 0.05× to 1.0×) [1].
* **Concurrency limits:**
  * Maximum concurrency across the entire eval-fleet defaults to 50 concurrent probes (acceptable range: 1 to 200) [1].
  * Backfill concurrency per model must be $\le 15$ [1].
* **Data retention:** Backfill traces and probe artifacts are retained for 90 days in the backfill archive (acceptable range: 14 to 365 days) [1].

SDK contract evolution and migration guide Overview:

This page documents Redwood's recommended strategy for evolving SDK contracts (public client APIs, CLI flags, response shapes) while minimizing customer impact. It covers principles, a repeatable migration workflow, testing and automation, rollout controls, and standard communication artifacts (deprecation notice, PR template, migration checklist). The guidance applies to all officially supported language SDKs, the CLI, and code snippets published on docs.redwood.ai.

Goals:
- Keep breaking changes as rare and well-signaled as possible.
- Provide a low-effort migration path for customers and internal integrators.
- Ensure docs, CI, and telemetry reflect live compatibility guarantees.
- Make rollbacks safe and fast.

Scope and definitions:
- "Contract": public surface exported by an SDK or CLI (function signatures, default values, enums, JSON response fields).
- "Minor compatibility": additive changes (new optional params, new fields in responses).
- "Major compatibility": incompatible change requiring client updates (removed or renamed params, changed return shapes).
- "Compatibility window": time between first deprecation notice and removal. Standard window is 90 days unless otherwise approved.

Principles:
1) Semantic versioning by intent: minor patches for fixes, minor versions for additive changes, major versions for breaking changes.
2) Dual-path rollout: when possible, keep legacy behavior available via a flag or compatibility toggle for the compatibility window.
3) Docs-first: update docs/SDK samples and central snippet registry in the same PR as code changes.
4) CI and telemetry: every SDK release must run the compatibility test suite and publish compatibility metrics.
5) Customer empathy: issue deprecation notices that include impact, migration steps, and an automated compatibility checker where feasible.
